#9232. UK government places export ban on Mughal calligraphy works valued at £900,000

The Mughal-era calligraphy albums were sold by Islamic and Indian art specialist dealer AeR Gallery in London

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

The UK government has temporarily blocked two 16th-century volumes of Mughal calligraphy from being taken out of the country permanently.

The export bar, which allows time for a UK gallery or institution to acquire the calligraphy works, will initially expire on 15 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £900,000, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

“By keeping the volumes in the country, it is hoped researchers can study how the construction of such calligraphic collections has evolved. Given so few works of this kind survive intact, its preservation makes it especially valuable,” says a statement from the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS). The volumes were kept in a private collection from the 1980s until 2020 when they were sold at Sotheby’s London for £620,000 (before fees) to a specialist dealer in London.

The calligraphic works, thought to be over 400 years old, are spread across 29 leaves and feature gold ornamentation of plant and animal motifs. The two volumes derive from an imperial album created around 1595-1605.

According to the DCMS statement, the original album was prepared for Mughal Emperor Akbar or his son Prince Salim at the royal workshop either in Lahore or Agra. Muhammad Hussain Kashmiri and Abd al-Rahim al-Haravi are among the calligraphers featured.

The Black Prince marble bust by Michael Rysbrack (around 1735)

Courtesy Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport

Meanwhile another export bar has been placed on a marble bust of the 14th-century prince Edward of Woodstock, the son of King Edward III of England and popularly known as the Black Prince. Created around 1735, the sculpture was made by the Flemish sculptor, Michael Rysbrack.

This export bar will initially expire on 5 February 2027, after which the owners will have 15 business days to consider any offers at the recommended price of £496,044 plus VAT, followed by a second deferral period of four months.

Fiona Twycross, the heritage minister, says in a statement: “For nearly three hundred years [the sculpture] has shaped how we tell the story of our medieval history and I hope that in a public gallery in the UK it can tell that story much more powerfully for many more years to come.”

#9231. North Korea Releases Outrageous Propaganda Photos of Kim Jong Un and Daughter

North Korea Releases Outrageous Propaganda Photos of Kim Jong Un and Daughter

North Korean state media has published a series of propaganda photos starring supreme leader Kim Jong Un and his heir apparent daughter.

The rare images published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) have caused an online sensation thanks to Kim Jong Un’s outrageous pose: smoking a cigarette while sitting on a throne-like chair at a ski resort.

Kim watched as his daughter Ju Ae (although her name has never been officially confirmed) hit the slopes, smiling as she carved the snow.

The photos were taken by KCNA over the weekend, capturing Kim Jong Un and his daughter visiting Samjiyon, a tourist town that’s being built close to the Chinese border. Under construction are Samjiyon airport, a tourist railway line, and a ski resort.

According to KCNA, Kim pronounced the resort’s hotels, lodges​, and housing “flawless and worthy of top marks.”

That his daughter, Ju Ae, features prominently in the photos is telling. South Korean intelligence believes she has been selected as his heir. She is thought to be 13 years old and still in training to take over the Kim dynasty that has ruled North Korea with an iron fist for almost 80 years. She would be the fourth Kim and the first female if she were to succeed her father.

North Korean state media does not publish photos accidentally, and the fact that Ju Ae has been photographed standing shoulder to shoulder with her father carries symbolic weight.

The internet lapped up the North Korean propaganda photos, saying that despotic Kim has “aura.”

The aura is actually ridiculous https://t.co/CV7HgBNABF

— Kangmin Lee | 이강민 (@kangminlee) November 17, 2026

News.com.au reports that people on X (formerly Twitter) joked that he’s “just like any other dad” and that he looks “super relaxed.”

“He looks genuinely happy and like he is having a great time,” another person said. But other people pointed out that bringing an armchair and table out on the snow is “just pure absurdity.”

#9229. Hasselblad X2D II Photographers Can Now Shoot Tethered Into Capture One

Hasselblad X2D II Photographers Can Now Shoot Tethered Into Capture One

Capture One and Hasselblad have jointly announced that real-time, wired tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C is now supported in Capture One with the latest versions of the camera’s firmware and Capture One software.

Tethered shooting support was announced as in the works back in July when Hasselblad first revealed its partnership with Capture One.

“There is a well-documented history between Hasselblad and Phase One, and we’re not here to dwell on it. Capture One has operated as an independent company since 2020, and what matters to us is serving photographers,” Capture One’s CEO Rafael Orta told PetaPixel last summer. “And they have asked us for this for years — on forums, in feature requests, in conversations. That’s why we’ve been working for a while with the Hasselblad team to deliver their shooters a native Capture One workflow.”

Now, not only can Hasselblad photographers edit their X2D II RAW files inside of Capture One, the full studio workflow is supported through tethering. Each image will appear on screen at full resolution at nearly the same moment it is captured when connected with a USB tethering cable. Hasselblad says that photographers can check focus and exposure while the set is still live and nobody has moved.

“[That] means no waiting around or breaking the flow. The full Capture One toolset is available from the first shot, so the grades and masks photographers apply to the first frame carry over to all subsequent shots,” Hasselblad says.

Studio photographers don’t need any convincing as to the value of tethering, but those who are less familiar might not know that the capability is hugely important for commercial sets where clients are on hand. It’s far easier to set clients at a digital tech workstation watching a monitor as results come in rather than hovering over a photographer’s shoulder trying to get a look at the rear LCD.

“This means creative direction and collaboration happen in real time, turning every session into a truly collaborative shoot,” the two companies add.

“We are always listening to our photographers, and tethering support for Hasselblad cameras was one of the top requests when our collaboration with Capture One was announced earlier this year,” Bronius Rudnickas, Global Marketing Manager at Hasselblad, says. “We are delighted that this workflow option is now available, giving Hasselblad photographers and creatives worldwide greater flexibility in their creative journeys.”

Wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C is available starting today in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Mobile 4.3.0, requiring X2D II 100C firmware version 1.4.15.7.

A primary beneficiary is the person or entity you designate to receive an asset — such as a life insurance policy, 401(k), IRA, or bank account — when you die. If you name multiple primary beneficiaries, they split the asset according to the percentages you specify. A contingent beneficiary (also called a secondary or backup beneficiary) receives the asset only if all primary beneficiaries are unable to inherit, either because they predeceased you, disclaimed the inheritance, or cannot be located.

This layered system exists because life is unpredictable. If you name your spouse as primary beneficiary on your life insurance and you both die in the same accident, the contingent beneficiary ensures the proceeds go where you intended rather than into your general estate where they become subject to probate.

You can name individuals, trusts, charities, or even your estate as a beneficiary. However, naming your estate is generally a poor choice because it forces the asset through probate, exposing it to creditors, delays, and court costs. The entire purpose of a beneficiary designation is to transfer assets outside of probate — naming your estate defeats that advantage.

When naming multiple beneficiaries, you must choose a distribution method that determines what happens if one beneficiary dies before you. This choice is critical and frequently misunderstood.

Per stirpes (Latin for "by the branch") means each branch of your family tree receives its designated share. If your son predeceases you, his share passes down to his children (your grandchildren) in equal portions. The family branch stays intact.

Per capita (Latin for "by the head") means assets are divided equally among surviving beneficiaries only. If your son predeceases you, his share is redistributed among your other surviving beneficiaries — his children receive nothing.

For most families, per stirpes is the safer default because it prevents accidental disinheritance of grandchildren. If you want surviving beneficiaries to absorb the shares of those who predecease you, per capita achieves that — but make sure that outcome aligns with your actual wishes.

Some financial institutions also offer per capita at each generation, which distributes equally among the nearest living generation first, then passes remaining shares equally to the next generation. This hybrid approach is less common but available at some custodians.

Beneficiary designations are deceptively simple forms that create binding legal consequences. The most expensive mistakes happen not from malice but from neglect.

In most states, a divorce does not automatically remove your ex-spouse from beneficiary designations on retirement accounts or life insurance policies. Federal law (ERISA) governs employer-sponsored plans like 401(k)s, and ERISA does not recognize state divorce revocation statutes. If you divorce and never update your 401(k) beneficiary, your ex-spouse can legally claim the entire balance — even if your will leaves everything to your new spouse.

Minor children cannot legally receive life insurance proceeds or retirement account distributions. If you name a 5-year-old as beneficiary, the insurance company will not release funds until a court appoints a guardian or conservator of the child's property. This process costs $2,000 to $5,000 in legal fees, takes months, and requires ongoing court reporting. Instead, name a trust for the benefit of the child or use your state's Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) custodial designation.

If you leave the beneficiary field blank or all named beneficiaries predecease you without a contingent, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This triggers probate, adds 6 to 18 months of delay, and exposes the asset to estate creditors. Always name at least one contingent beneficiary.

Your beneficiary designations and your will can contradict each other. The beneficiary designation always wins. If your will says your daughter gets your IRA but the IRA beneficiary form still names your brother, your brother gets the IRA. Review both documents together annually.

Set a recurring calendar reminder to review every beneficiary designation once per year — ideally alongside your tax preparation. Pull statements from your 401(k), IRA, life insurance, bank accounts, and brokerage accounts. Verify that primary and contingent designations match your current wishes. This 30-minute annual review prevents the kind of outdated-beneficiary disasters that lead to costly litigation and assets going to unintended recipients.

Yes. You can name multiple primary beneficiaries and assign a percentage to each. For example, you could name three children as primary beneficiaries at 33.3% each. The percentages must total 100%.

If all primary beneficiaries predecease you and no contingent is named, the asset typically defaults to your estate. This forces the asset through probate, where it is subject to creditor claims, court costs, and delays of 6 to 18 months.

For state-law-governed accounts like IRAs and life insurance, some states have revocation-upon-divorce statutes — but not all. For ERISA-governed accounts like employer 401(k)s, federal law does not recognize state divorce revocation. You must manually update the beneficiary form after divorce to be safe.

Yes. A beneficiary can file a qualified disclaimer within 9 months of the account holder's death. The disclaimed asset then passes to the contingent beneficiary or according to the plan's default rules. Disclaimers are sometimes used for tax planning purposes.

Naming a trust provides control over how and when assets are distributed — especially useful for minor children, spendthrift beneficiaries, or blended families. However, trusts named as IRA beneficiaries must meet specific IRS requirements to qualify for stretch distributions under the SECURE Act. Consult an estate planning attorney before naming a trust as retirement account beneficiary.

A POD designation on a bank account functions exactly like a beneficiary designation. The named person receives the account balance upon your death without going through probate. You maintain full control of the account during your lifetime and can change the POD beneficiary at any time.

Primary and contingent beneficiary designations are among the most powerful — and most overlooked — estate planning tools. They transfer assets instantly upon death, bypass probate entirely, and override your will in every state. The 30 minutes it takes to review and update your designations after every major life event can save your family months of legal proceedings, thousands in attorney fees, and the heartbreak of assets going to unintended recipients.

#9226. LeBron James Sues Sports-Betting App for Using AI-Generated Images of Him

LeBron James Sues Sports-Betting App for Using AI-Generated Images of Him

NBA superstar LeBron James has sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app for allegedly using AI-generated images of him in its marketing.

On Tuesday, James filed a lawsuit in the Southern District of New York against the founders of Bron, an AI-powered sports-betting app. The lawsuit focuses on a video ad released by the Bron app’s founders earlier this month. It shows an AI-generated version of James using the Bron app to bet on basketball games from a locker room.

According to the complaint, the ad depicts James wearing a basketball jersey bearing his nickname and the iconic number 23. It also reproduces his tattoos and a simulated version of his voice. The video shows the AI-generated figure scrolling through NBA betting options on the app.

“The ad catapulted the Bron app from obscurity to controversy, with the ad gaining a million views within a day — exactly as defendants intended,” James argues in the civil complaint, according to a report by Courthouse News Service.

The complaint also says the AI-generated image of the basketball star “falsely communicates that Mr. James wagers, or considers wagering, on NBA games and NBA player ​performance—conduct that NBA rules prohibit.”

James argues that the depiction of him sitting in a locker room and betting on basketball could also harm his reputation.

“This is at odds with Mr. James’s well-known and highly televised routine of being on time for games and being one of the first people out on the court,” he argues.

James also claims that the app’s name was chosen to attract attention by exploiting his well-known “Bron” nickname. He accuses PlayVision, the company that operates the app, and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, of deliberately using the name to mislead consumers into thinking he endorsed or was affiliated with the product.

James’s lawyers sent the company a cease-and-desist letter on November 5. Following the letter, the startup removed the ad from X (the platform formerly known as Twitter) and Instagram and said it was working to change the app’s name, according to the complaint. However, the lawsuit alleges that the video remained available through third-party reposts and that the company had not changed the app’s name by the time the lawsuit was filed.

LeBron’s lawsuit comes after Norwegian soccer player Erling Haaland sued an airline last month over a social media post that featured an edited image referencing his distinctive hairstyle during the 2026 World Cup.

#9225. New bi-national art initiative reframes stereotypes about Mexico-US border

Exterior view of Azul Arena in Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, with mural ¡Pásele, pásele! by LxsDos Courtesy of Azul Arena, 2025

Can the “open wound” of the Mexico-US border be healed? Sutura, a new bi-national art programme in Ciudad Juárez, Chihuahua, and El Paso, Texas (18 November-22 November), looks beyond stereotypes of violence surrounding the Mexico-US border and explores how art might help mend the region’s many wounds, even imperfectly or temporarily. Sutura (Spanish for “suture”) brings together more than 100 artists across 20 venues, including the El Paso Museum of Art (EPMA), the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and the Museo de Arte de Ciudad Juárez (MACJ), alongside independent projects and pop-up exhibitions.

Juárez has long been associated with sensational narratives of violence. Persistent migration issues, heightened by stricter border controls and alarming deportation measures, feminicides, the drug war and hyper-surveillance have shaped the local context. These aspects have permeated cultural production. “Endless works have explored this territory as a symbol and symptom of an apocalyptic future,” writes Willivaldo Delgadillo in his book-length essay Fabular Juárez (2020).

Though seemingly worlds apart today, Ciudad Juárez and El Paso were one city until the Rio Grande river was established as the border between Mexico and the US in 1848. Despite tensions between their respective countries, the two cities are still connected by education, jobs and transit.

“On each side of the border, nuanced and contrasting fears and ideologies coexist, but there is also community,” Edgar Picazo Merino, Sutura’s founder and lead organiser, tells The Art Newspaper. “For all of us who live here, the border is a personal, lived experience.” Picazo founded the independent initiative Azul Arena in 2019 to support the Juárez-El Paso art scene; it established a permanent space in Juárez in 2022.

Central to thinking about the border in the context of Sutura and more broadly is Chicana writer Gloria Anzaldúa’s 1987 metaphor of the border as an “open wound”. “The Third World grates against the first and bleeds,” Anzaldúa wrote. “And before a scab forms, it haemorrhages again, the lifeblood of two worlds merging to form a third country—a border culture.” The “open wound” concept has become commonplace in border literature, Picazo says, while Sutura seeks to deconstruct it: “If the border is a wound, how can the arts suture its many wounds, while opening places of reflection and interaction?”

Detail of Justin Favela's Mantecore (White Tiger) (2017), featured in Qué tanto es tantito, a group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso

Sutura builds on binational initiatives like Insite, which emerged in 1992 at the San Diego-Tijuana border and initially featured site-specific installations before changing formats. It also draws on regional ties. The Juárez-El Paso Border Biennial, launched in 2008 by the EPMA and MACJ, is currently in its eighth edition, Imagining the Border (until 2 May 2027). Co-curated by the Juárez-based curators Adriana Miramontes Olivas and Alejandro Morales, it features more than 80 works by artists based within 300 miles of El Paso and Juárez.

“A border that is always there, one that weighs heavily on our communities, rarely lets us imagine it,” Morales says. “This edition opens that space, offering a plural and rigorous portrait of it as living territory.”

The Border Biennial has strived to shift perceptions. “The biennial has national relevance, moving beyond portrayals of the border as perpetually on fire, highlighting its creative richness and cultural legacies,” says Edward Hayes Jr, the director of the EPMA, adding that the project requires overcoming diplomatic and logistical challenges. “We aim for the biennial to be a structural project for both institutions,” says Christian Diego Diego, MACJ’s director. Diego adds that over its past and current editions, the Border Biennial has featured more than 400 works by around 270 artists, “reflecting the border’s ambivalence and multiple stories”. Sutura’s programme includes visits to the biennial, reflecting dialogue with the artists, curators and venues.

Sutura also grew from asking how a Juárez-El Paso art week might unfold. Border initiatives are gaining visibility. The fair Material, through its two-year Projects programme, has supported Azul Arena and the Juárez curatorial duo Un Dique with mentorship and free participation in its Mexico City and Guadalajara fairs. Un Dique joins Sutura by curating theexhibition Border Kaijus on border hypervigilance. Two other border cities have recently created art weeks amid growing efforts to decentralise a national scene largely centred on Mexico City: Tijuana held its second art week in July; Mexicali held its first in April.

“There is a growing scene among border Mexican cities with spaces and initiatives interacting,” says Andres Payan Estrada, the director and chief curator of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts and Sutura’s artistic strategy director. Still, he adds, Sutura is not an art week: “It is a non-commercial collaborative initiative with a strong community component.”

Installation view of the group show Costuras Territoriales at the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso Courtesy of the Stanlee and Gerald Rubin Center for the Visual Arts at the University of Texas, El Paso

In El Paso, institutional participation is strong. During Sutura, the Rubin Center is showing Costuras Territoriales (until 12 December), curated by Payan and featuring textile-inspired works by five women artists connected to the border, including Teresa Margolles, Tania Candiani and Juárez-based Olga Guerra. “The way in which artists explore the border has sometimes become a cliché,” Guerra says. “I intend to reflect relationality through a more poetic approach, incorporating locally found organic materials and fibres, along with reused materials.”

Independent initiatives are vital in Juárez, where conventional galleries are non-existent. Picazo’s Azul Arena, a pillar of the city’s scene, will present the exhibition En la línea, exploring the line as a metaphor for the border. The Juárez-based artist Haydee Alonso, co-founder of San Luis Contemporáneo, will curate the exhibition ¿Qué tanto es tantito? there and present a performance at Azul Arena. “My work analyses transborder relations through the body and objects, opening spaces within the complexities of living here,” says Alonso, who crosses the border daily to teach at the University of Texas at El Paso. Both projects have received support from the Mellon Foundation, which Alonso and Picazo consider crucial to local initiatives. In El Paso, where independent spaces are relatively scarce, The Falstaff, a community-centred hybrid art space, will host exhibitions and concerts.

Installation view ofthe group exhibiton Qué tanto es tantito, group show on view at San Luis Contemporáneo, Ciudad Juárez Courtesy Haydee Alonso

Sutura also supports the local scene by showcasing six El Paso and Juárez projects selected through an open call, with each project receiving $3,000 for production costs. The photography exhibition Relatos de la Frontera: Cuerpo y Espacio explores border perspectives through the body and space Another show, Tierra Suelta, presents works inspired by children of migrant families that settled in Juárez for reasons other than the “American dream”, integrating a community activation into the programme. These projects foreground local perspectives in a region often depicted by outsiders, alongside established artists—primarily Mexican and Mexican American—whose work reflects on the border.

Picazo acknowledges the complexities of a bi-national event: not everyone can cross both ways because of visa restrictions and other issues. “The programme has parallel activities so you can experience Sutura even from one side of the border,” he says.

Sutura speaks more of resilience than crisis, more of possibility than scarcity.“Historically, the border is explained one-dimensionally, yet a myriad of dynamics co-exist here,” Picazo says. “Sutura exists as a relational art encounter.”

It’s the first physical iteration of the El Paso and Juárez exhibition in five years, after the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic shut down the 2020 edition

#9222. Photographer Encounters Legendary Grizzly Bear Known as ‘The Boss’ Ahead of Hibernation

Photographer Encounters Legendary Grizzly Bear Known as ‘The Boss’ Ahead of Hibernation

A photographer had an incredible encounter with a famous grizzly bear known as “The Boss” in Banff, Canada.

Jason Leo Bantle was in Banff National Park when he came across fresh bear tracks in the snow. Knowing the big bruin must be in the area, Bantle came back on November 6 and spotted The Boss foraging along the railway tracks that run through the park.

“Known for grains being dropped from railcars or other animals being hit, The Boss has learned that when food is not plentiful in the backcountry, the tracks may offer some subsistence,” Bantle tells PetaPixel.

Bantle is aware of the risks of approaching a grizzly in the wild, so he waited at a great distance, observing the bear through an 840mm telephoto lens and binoculars.

The New York Times ran an article over the weekend about The Boss. It revealed that he is categorized as “habituated” by the park’s management, which means he is not bothered by people so long as he is left alone.

“The biggest thing is his gentleness and his respect towards the people,” Paul Klra, a gas station owner and photographer, told The Times. “He has never done any harm to anyone.”

While The Boss has never done any harm to humans, he certainly has done harm to other bears. His biggest rival in the area is a bear called Split Lip; The Boss gave him that lip.

He’s also survived being struck by a train and has been known to kill and eat black bears. However, a park ecologist tells The Times that 90% of The Boss’s diet is made up of berries, roots, and other plants.

“As a professional photographer, you are focused on your craft and capturing an image that is the essence of the animal and their environment, so you do lose yourself in the moment,” Bantle says of photographing The Boss.

“I always reflect back on moments like this with The Boss; he is a living legend! The one image of him as he lumbered toward me with light snow falling was just magnificent: the grandeur of this bear, an apex predator, yet the gentleness of his quiet presence — no wind and a light snowfall, it was humbling to be in his presence.”

The Boss is thought to be 28 years old, advanced for a bear. He has become internationally famous, and it makes the news when he comes out of hibernation.

#9220. Researchers Film Gorillas Forming a ‘Living Ladder’ to Reach High Branch

Researchers Film Gorillas Forming a ‘Living Ladder’ to Reach High Branch

Scientists captured extraordinary footage of two gorillas climbing on each other’s backs and forming a “living ladder” to reach a high branch on a tree that was out of reach.

The pair of female western lowland gorillas were filmed displaying what researchers describe as rare behavior in their species: one positioned herself to provide a stable platform while the other climbed onto her back to reach vegetation they could not access individually.

Researchers from Tel Aviv University documented the behavior at the Ramat Gan Safari in Israel, recording three separate instances of spontaneous cooperation between the adult gorillas. According to a study published in the journal Primates, the events took place in 2021, 2024, and 2025 and involved the same two half-sisters, Amelia and Lisha.

In each instance, the gorillas performed the same roles. Lisha provided a stable platform, while Amelia climbed onto her back to reach nearby branches. Neither animal had been trained to perform the behavior.

The most extensively documented event occurred in September 2024, when keepers noticed the two females peacefully eating bark and leaves from a large branch that had previously been beyond their reach. To find out how they had accessed the food, staff reviewed security camera footage.

The recordings revealed a coordinated series of actions. Amelia first walked over and climbed onto a rock beneath a Peltophorum dubium tree. Lisha then joined her, standing firmly on all fours on the rock. Amelia climbed onto Lisha’s back, stood upright, and stretched upward to grasp and break off a branch approximately 15 feet above the ground.

The combination of the rock, Lisha’s stable position, and Amelia’s additional height allowed her to reach the branch. An electric barrier around the tree trunk prevented the gorillas from climbing it directly.

Michael Levitzky, who initiated and led the study, says the footage shows genuine cooperation, with Leisha independently choosing to help Amelia achieve their shared goal rather than simply being used as a tool.

“When I first watched the footage, it was clear to me that this was something extraordinary. What I find fascinating is that Leisha did more than simply serve as a ‘step’ for Amelia,” Levitzky says in a statement. “She appeared to participate actively and willingly in solving the problem, approaching on her own initiative and positioning herself in exactly the right place, without Amelia physically guiding her. This is the difference between using another individual as a tool and true cooperation, in which both individuals work together toward the same goal.

Levitzky says that gorillas may be more socially and cognitively intelligent than previously thought, and that further research could reveal more about how they cooperate and what this tells us about the origins of cooperation in humans.

“For years, gorillas were considered less cognitively sophisticated than other great apes,” Levitzky explains. “As more observations like these accumulate, we will be able to deepen and refine our understanding of their social and cognitive abilities. Future studies involving systematic documentation and audio recordings could help us decipher how they coordinate with one another, and perhaps also teach us something about the roots of cooperation in our own species.”

#9217. Instagram’s New Tool Helps Creators Assert Their Rights

Instagram’s New Tool Helps Creators Assert Their Rights

Instagram is rolling out a new tool designed to help creators identify and manage unauthorized copies of their videos, as the platform responds to growing concerns about content theft and the use of AI to reproduce original work.

The feature is called Content Protection, and it allows eligible creators to monitor copies of their videos across Instagram and Facebook and decide how to respond when a match is detected. Meta previously introduced a similar tool on Facebook and is now bringing the feature to Instagram.

Once enrolled, creators will receive alerts when Instagram identifies a visual match of one of their original videos. They can then choose to monitor the copied video’s performance, hide it from Instagram and Facebook, add an attribution link directing viewers to the original video, or release their claim and allow the content to remain on the platform.

TechCrunch reports that creators who enroll will have new original videos automatically protected. They can also manually select eligible videos published before enrolling. Accounts that have permission to use a creator’s work, such as a second profile or a brand account, can be added to an allow list to prevent their content from being flagged.

Instagram is also expanding its detection capabilities to address AI-generated content. The platform will begin testing a feature that identifies videos using audio from a creator’s original work, including spoken words, even when the original visuals have been replaced with AI-generated imagery.

The company says it is also exploring ways to limit the reach of accounts and content that repeatedly use AI tools to repurpose other creators’ work.

The rollout comes as creators face increasing difficulties protecting their material from AI-generated copies. Videos featuring altered faces, fictional performers, and recreated comedy routines have become a growing concern, particularly for creators whose work is reused without attribution.

Comedian Sarah Purdum tells Mashable she discovered her material had been repurposed by an AI account.

“It seems to be that female comedians’ work is being stolen and repurposed for sexy AI models,” she says. “I feel annoyed that my work is being taken for the purpose of drawing in men.”

#9216. Nan Goldin to debut new film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

For audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

What links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

The show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a new score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

It accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

Elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian

For Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027

#9214. Mitakon’s $599 Medium-Format 65mm f/1.4 II Is Lighter and Upgrades Its Bokeh

Mitakon’s $599 Medium-Format 65mm f/1.4 II Is Lighter and Upgrades Its Bokeh

Way back in 2018, Zhongyi (ZY) Optics launched the Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 manual-focus lens for the Fujifilm GFX mirrorless camera system. Now there’s an upgraded Mark II version, which is still ultra-fast, manual-focus, and very affordable. It’s also available for Hasselblad cameras.

The Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is lighter than its predecessor, has a new aperture diaphragm, and features an upgraded metal design.

The optical design is unchanged, with the lens still sporting 11 elements arranged across seven groups. ZY Optics says the lens, which has two High Refractive Index (HRI) and two Ultra-Low Dispersion (UD) elements, delivers “exceptional image quality” with minimized chromatic aberrations.

However, behind the glass is a new 11-bladed aperture diaphragm, up from a nine-bladed unit in the original Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4. ZY Optics says the new circular diaphragm delivers “rounder bokeh highlights.”

With its f/1.4 aperture, the lens is still among the very fastest available for the Fujifilm GFX system. Fujifilm itself doesn’t make any lenses quite as fast—its fastest options are the GF 55mm f/1.7 R WR and the GF 80mm f/1.7, both of which cost over $2,000.

Over on the Hasselblad X system, it’s a similar story. Hasselblad’s fastest lens is the XCD 1,9/80, or, put in more common terms, an 80mm f/1.9 lens. The company’s 65mm prime is the XCD 2,8/65.

Granted, Fujifilm’s and Hasselblad’s lenses are also native and equipped with autofocus, so there’s that. ZY Optics targets a different market, one less concerned with autofocus and looking to save some money.

The manual-focus prime can focus as close as 0.7 meters (2.3 feet), resulting in a maximum magnification of about 0.25x. Its 65mm focal length delivers a full-frame equivalent of just over 51mm.

Compared to its predecessor, the Mark II lens is significantly lighter. Weighing 900 grams (31.7 ounces), it sheds about 150 grams (5.3 ounces) compared to the original. The lens measures 95 millimeters (3.74 inches) long, accepts a 67mm filter thread, and features a built-in retractable lens hood.

ZY Optics says the new lens has an improved, precision-machined metal barrel. It looks a little different overall but retains the same general design, with a wide, ridged focus ring and an aperture control ring near the front of the lens. The depth-of-field scale markings have changed slightly, too.

The ZY Optics Mitakon Speedmaster 65mm f/1.4 II is available now for Fujifilm GFX and Hasselblad X mounts for $599.

#9211. Canon Warns That Lenses Can Detach Suddenly From Its Teleconverters

Canon Warns That Lenses Can Detach Suddenly From Its Teleconverters

Regional Canon offices worldwide have issued an urgent service notice regarding the company’s RF1.4x and RF2x extenders, commonly known as teleconverters. Canon warns that if users suspect anything unusual about how their extender feels in use, they should request an inspection and repair through Canon.

Canon Rumors claims this is a known issue with Canon RF-mount extenders, where a lens can feel like it is locked onto the extender even when it isn’t. In some cases, a lens could even detach from the extender and fall to the ground. Given that extenders are commonly used with expensive telephoto lenses, this could be an extremely costly problem.

Canon Malaysia’s notice on the matter is particularly interesting, offering slightly more information than the service notice from Canon U.S.A. and others.

“We regret to inform that a potential issue has been confirmed for Extender RF1.4x/RF2x,” Canon Malaysia says, which goes further than what Canon U.S.A. writes.

Canon U.S.A. stops short of mentioning any issue, only issuing a “service notice” and noting that Canon RF extender users should always check the following:

Canon U.S.A. adds that if photographers notice “anything unusual,” which could include the lens release lever feeling “stiff” or like it is “catching on something and cannot be operated smoothly,” there is a chance the RF lens is not locked in place.

“If used in this state, the RF lens may come off,” Canon continues.

Any affected users, or those who have any concerns about the operation of their RF extenders, should contact the Canon Customer Support Center in their region for an inspection and, if necessary, a free repair.

In any case, it is not immediately clear what the exact issue is, what causes it, or how it might be fixed. Given that Canon is offering free repairs, though, it is reasonable to speculate that there is a physical component that needs to be fixed to ensure the consistently safe operation of Canon RF extenders.

Any photographers with Canon RF extenders should carefully inspect them before use and, if worried at all, contact their local Canon customer support team. A lens falling off an extender is a significant risk.

PetaPixel has reached out to Canon for comment and will update this story if it hears back.

As rumours about the casting of the next James Bond began to hot up this week, my phone has been busy. Most of my friends (hello, both!) know me as a huge James Bond fan, and have wanted to know who I thought was going to get the role. Well, one thing's for sure, I told them all. It won't be Pattinson. Mark my words. He's just too famous.

So you can imagine my surprise when Robert Pattinson was indeed announced as the new James Bond this afternoon. Everything about the news feels bizarre to me, including the lack of press release and associated fanfare (whereas Daniel Craig rode down the Thames on a speedboat, Pattinson was announced via a simple social media post). But the biggest shock is that Pattinson is by far the most famous person to be cast in the role. He's the first bonafide A-lister to pick up the Walther PPK. He's Batman, for God's sake. For better or worse, the Bond brand changed forever today. And it's thanks to one name: Amazon.

It perhaps isn't surprising that Blofeld's—sorry, Bezos's—company has opted for such a bankable star. The company paid billions to acquire MGM (which owned the rights to Bond), and will want a return on its investment. But the whole thing seems so at odds with the ethos of the previous Bond custodians. "I felt I had to have an unknown actor, not a star," producer Cubby Broccoli said of the search for the very first Bond. "Above all, a man you’d believe could be James Bond."

For decades, Bond has been one of the most carefully controlled brands in entertainment. The gun barrel sequence, the theme tune, the 007 logo, the Aston Martin; every element is instantly recognisable, and has been meticulously protected by the Broccoli family. Bond films have always felt like events, partly because they don't come along very often. But Amazon doesn't do scarcity, it does content. And with the company now in creative control of the franchise, it's hard not to wonder how long it will be before 007 becomes less of a cinematic institution and more of an endlessly expandable IP. I'm not sure I'm ready for the 'Young Q' spin-off.

There are, of course, opportunities here. Bond has arguably been in need of a shake-up for some time, and Pattinson is a genuinely exciting actor, capable of bringing something strange, unpredictable and perhaps even uncomfortable to a character that has occasionally felt trapped by his own iconography. But the choice also feels like a statement of intent from Amazon. Where previous Bond actors were largely blank canvases onto which the 007 identity could be projected, Pattinson arrives with a huge, established brand of his own. Rather than making a star out of Bond, Amazon has bought a star to sell Bond. It's a subtle distinction, but a significant one. Am I going to be able to look up at the screen and see James Bond, rather than Robert Pattinson in a suit?

But while it'll be Pattinson's name that hogs the headlines, the bigger question isn't simply what kind of Bond Pattinson will be, but what kind of brand Amazon wants Bond to become. Will the company recognise that Bond's enduring appeal lies partly in his exclusivity, his mystique, and his ability to remain just a little out of reach? For all of his reinventions, 007 has always felt bigger than the actor playing him. Until today.

#9208. Customizable and Colorful (Not Boring) Camera Nominated for iPhone App of the Year

Customizable and Colorful (Not Boring) Camera Nominated for iPhone App of the Year

Apple announced its 2026 App Store Award finalists today, and a standout iPhone camera app earned a coveted nomination.

(Not Boring) Camera is one of three finalists for iPhone App of the Year, and it’s easy to see why. The app, sometimes stylized as !Camera, features a fully 3D camera interface, extensive customization, and haptic feedback designed to replicate the feel of holding an actual camera.

“You’re gonna love how it feels,” says the app’s developer, Not Boring. “I guarantee it.”

(Not Boring) Camera aims to be more than just a pretty face, though. Like other popular iPhone camera apps released in recent years, !Camera eschews AI processing in favor of a more natural imaging engine. Its proprietary SuperRaw mode promises “film-like tones” while preserving a photo’s “beautiful natural grain.”

The app supports Apple’s ProRAW and Basic processing, plus it can save photos as RAW DNG files for editing in other apps, like Darkroom, Lightroom, and Photoshop. It also supports HDR image capture across four settings: off, low, medium, and high.

“!Camera is the first camera app to enable professional-level color grading with 3D LUTs (‘lookup tables’) used in high-end workflows by pro photographers to achieve realistic film simulations and unique cinematic looks,” Not Boring continues. The app includes photographer-designed LUTs, LUT importing, and preset creation tools. The company regularly releases new styles and collaborations.

The most recent collaboration is with the Tokyo-based art collective Nuevo.Tokyo. The AgBr style brings a vintage-inspired black-and-white look to !Camera.

The app also packs extensive manual controls—including exposure, shutter speed, white balance, ISO, and focus—alongside tools like focus peaking, zebra stripes, and a histogram. For finer focus adjustments, the virtual lens features its own “Precision Focus Ring” with a focus scale.

Customization extends to the look of the camera app itself. Users can design a custom virtual camera by choosing colors for its body, top panel, lens, and buttons.

If (Not Boring) Camera ultimately wins the award when winners are announced next month, it certainly won’t be the first camera app to earn the honor. In 2024, Kino and Adobe Lightroom were both honored among Apple’s Apps of the Year. Halide Mark II won in 2022, too.

(Not Boring) Camera is available now for free. Access to all features requires a Plus membership, which is $14.99 per year or $59.99 for a lifetime license.

#9207. Sotheby’s makes last-minute deal to sell $180m Van Gogh painting following dispute

The Blaquier family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) in 1975

Sotheby’s today announced that a settlement has been reached over the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890). The work has been poised to achieve a record price for the artist but became the subject of a claim by the heirs of its Jewish former owners, who called for the work to be withdrawn from the 18 November auction in New York.

The Sotheby’s statement records that the auction house is “pleased to confirm that an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale of Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs”. The sale will now proceed as planned.

The work is estimated at around $180m ($207m with fees) and has been guaranteed by Sotheby's to sell. This is far in excess of the previous record of $117m, paid at Christie’s in 2022 for Van Gogh’s Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888).

The Blaquier-Arrieta family, from Argentina, bought Blossoming Chestnut Trees in 1975. As the Sotheby’s statement explains: “In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”

The provenance in the Sotheby’s catalogue entry notes, as it has done since last month, that the painting was acquired by the Berlin publisher Samuel Fischer and his wife Hedwig in 1909. Their son-in-law, Gottfried Bermann Fischer, deposited the Van Gogh with the Amsterdam gallery Paul Cassirer in 1932 or 1933—and it was then bought by Paris collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in 1936.

Last Thursday (12 November), in a surprise move, the Berlin-based restitution researcher Gunnar Schnabel sent a letter to Sotheby’s, on behalf of the Fischer heirs. He questioned the 1936 sale—which he says took place three months after the family had left Berlin for Vienna—asking Sotheby’s to prove that the picture had been sold at its market value and that its sale was not forced. In the meantime, Schnabel asked for this week’s sale to be delayed.

In a statement, the Fischer heirs commented: “We are grateful for the trusting and fair negotiation and collaboration with Sotheby’s and the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which make it possible to acknowledge the suffering of the Fischer family during the Nazi era and honour Gisela Berman Fischer's [granddaughter of Samuel and Hedwig] history of seeking justice for her family.”

The Blaquier-Arrieta family commented: “We are pleased to have reached an amicable resolution with the Fischer heirs. We appreciate the constructive dialogue that made this resolution possible and look forward to an extraordinary result and to passing along this masterpiece to a new generation of collectors.”

No details have been released on the nature of the agreement and whether the Fischer family will receive financial compensation.

What impact, if any, the short-lived dispute will have on the sale will only become apparent with the bidding.

#9204. Lumix Has the Video Chops to Beat Sony, So Why Won’t It Even Try?

Lumix Has the Video Chops to Beat Sony, So Why Won’t It Even Try?

A couple of weeks ago, Jordan Drake texted me from the Lumix event in Osaka with the rundown on what was being announced. When he described the S1 II but in a box camera format, I couldn’t help but express my dismay. “That’s it?”

For context, this year is the 25th anniversary of the Lumix brand, and the company opened with the L10 back in May. That felt like a proper start to what we assumed would be a full year of serious product launches. This wasn’t an expectation we came in with; it was one that Lumix put into our heads: the company specifically said it had more planned for 2026 and that we should be excited.

And so I carried that excitement with me for the next six months, knowing we might not see that promise come to fruition until late fall. That is a major reason why I’m so disappointed by the SHX1. It’s not that the camera is bad or that it doesn’t have a core, dedicated audience. It’s more that this isn’t the camera that I was expecting to be the cap of a celebratory year where Lumix was poised to really strut its stuff.

The Lumix S1H has been languishing for years, and not because there isn’t a market for it. It just seems like Panasonic doesn’t know what to do with it. When the S1 II was announced last year, that really felt like the case because the camera felt like it did everything we ever wanted the S1H successor to do.

‘The FX3 is just the visual language of a semi-professional small camera now.’

But I argue that, even with all that known, Lumix — the brand known for video performance — has, for some reason, been unwilling to take on Sony in the highly competitive commercial camera space that is dominated by the FX series. For all of its strengths in video, Lumix appears scared: either of Sony or of the success that would come from actually trying.

In 2021, Sony announced the FX3 and, in one fell swoop, changed the game. It created the perfect camera for the mid- to high-end filmmaker at a really compelling sub-$4,000 price. It wasn’t part of the Alpha series, so Sony could fully focus on video performance. The FX3 is the logical conclusion to the success that the a7S series created, and it was (and still is) immensely popular.

As Jordan Drake put it in this week’s episode of The PetaPixel Podcast, the FX3 became the industry standard through its design.

“It became just the industry standard for if you’re doing event work or commercial work. Because it is such a recognizable camera – like that gray, with that pronounced, sharp-edged grip – when producers and directors and people see it, they immediately know that’s acceptable. That’s the big thing I think Panasonic’s butting up against. An S1 II is every bit as capable but it looks like an old DSLR. And I think everybody wants to move away from that,” he says.

“The FX3 is just the visual language of a semi-professional small camera now.”

Canon and Nikon got that memo, which is why the ZR and the R6V have that same visual design language. Panasonic Lumix has chosen to ignore that aspect of its cameras to its extreme detriment.

Compared to Sony, Panasonic’s camera division (it is now one division that combined Lumix and VariCam) is small, and maybe that’s to blame for these issues. Maybe it doesn’t have a good design department. That would make sense, since Lumix has not been a particularly good example of enticing camera design, and it’s very much hurting it now. I think it believes it should be able to stand out through performance alone, and that’s a lovely sentiment, but it’s just not reality.

Creators buy cameras that they want to be seen with, not just cameras that can do the job. You can argue that isn’t how it should be, but it is very much a reality.

There is nothing wrong with the SHX1. It’s an excellent camera that will resonate with current Lumix filmmakers. Maybe that’s what Lumix wants: to keep its current audience happy.

But that’s not what Lumix needs right now. To grow and find itself in more hands, Lumix needs to actually beat Sony at its own game – a game it is entirely equipped to win handily. I am a Lumix user and have been since the GH4. It’s reluctance to even try and take on the FX tier is incredibly disheartening, because I 100% would love to have an FX5-styled camera with Lumix guts.

Lumix’s in-body stabilization is better. Lumix’s record modes are, on the whole, better. I mean, the company was giving filmmakers open gate and in-camera anamorphic desqueeze years before it was even a twinkle in the other brands’ eyes. This is the space where Lumix should be king, but its refusal to go at Sony head-on makes it seem like the company is scared it might not succeed.

‘An S1 II is every bit as capable but it looks like an old DSLR. And I think everybody wants to move away from that.’

Or, worse, Lumix is scared of the success that would bring it. Maybe it doesn’t want that level of attention. Maybe it likes feeling like a scrappy underdog, and the idea of being a market leader is just too much pressure.

Whatever the case, as good as the SHX1 is, it’s not the camera Lumix needed to release in this moment. Sony was stumbling and tripping over itself with the FX5 launch, giving Lumix the perfect window to jump ahead if it were prepared for the moment. It clearly was not.

I get not being able to directly respond to the FX5, but the FX3? Five years later, how do you not respond to that? You, the video camera company? It feels like cowardice despite the timing not possibly being any better… which makes missing that moment even worse.

I don’t think Lumix fully grasps how badly they fumbled this opportunity. They might not realize the extent of this mistake for months or years. With the moment up for grabs, Lumix just chose not to reach out for it.

#9203. Harvard museum returns human remains to Brazil

Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, Cambridge, Massachusetts Photo: Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons

The Brazilian government held two ceremonies this month to mark the repatriation of the remains of two people of African descent taken from the country in the 19th century. The remains were transferred from the collection of Harvard University’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

The repatriation is part of a university initiative launched in 2019 to review historical records related to individuals of African descent from Brazil and the Caribbean islands. The review identified one person who is recorded as having been enslaved, while there is strong evidence that the other was as well.

The National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (Museu Nacional/UFRJ) received the skull of an adult woman, held at the Peabody Museum since 1870 following its transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. According to records, it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who accompanied the naturalist Louis Agassiz on an expedition to Brazil in 1865-66, serving as the mission’s photographer.

The skull was described in the records as the “skull of a negro”, with an accompanying note stating it had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro”, although circumstances surrounding its removal are still under investigation. The remains may have been taken from the Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground in Rio used for enslaved Africans who died after arriving in Brazil that operated in the 18th century and early 19th century. The burial ground was rediscovered in 1996 during construction work in the city’s port district.

The Museu Nacional/UFRJ will assume temporary custody of the skull, which will not be publicly displayed nor used for research, reproduction or other purposes. Researchers will undertake further work to establish the woman’s origins before decisions are made about the skull’s final destination.

A ceremony on 11 November at the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro to mark repatriation of the remains of an enslaved woman from the Peabody Museum at Harvard University Courtesy Ministério das Relações Exteriores, Brazil

“This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, the deputy director of the Museu Nacional/UFRJ, said during the ceremony in Rio on 11 November. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”

Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, noted that the repatriation represents a milestone in acknowledging the historical violence resulting from enslavement. “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognising the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” she said. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”

Meanwhile, the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador received the remains of an enslaved African man of Nagô origin. The man is believed to have participated in the Malê Revolt in Salvador in January 1835, a major uprising led by both enslaved and freed Africans against slavery and religious persecution in Brazil. He was reportedly wounded during the uprising and subsequently died in hospital in Salvador.

A 2022 report on Harvard’s museum collections documented the presence of thousands of human remains, prompting scrutiny of how they had been collected and studied. Neither the museum nor the university returned The Art Newspaper’s requests for comment.

More than four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil during the transatlantic slave trade, making it the largest destination for the forced migration of Africans across the Atlantic. The country was the last in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Records show how masters retained power over enslaved people even after emancipation

#9202. Olivia Reavey's Impromptu Sensuality

Everything is a treasured scrap for Reavey to pull from in her unorthodox black-and-white photography.

Olivia Reavey moves at breakneck speed. Her silver-gelatin-analog printing process is frenzied and intense: Black-and-white prints are cut into irregular quadrilaterals with crumpled edges, then hung unframed and loosely fixed to the walls with clips, pins, and other supports. But this is not just slapdash; everything here is intentionally energetic and playful, with images asserting the body’s formal pleasure captured in film.

Many bare their flesh but are often obfuscated or appear with objects: a broken branch covers a male’s buttocks in “Stick” (all works 2026); a wooden lever protrudes from a woman’s pubic area, captured in the reflection of a mirror in “Untitled.” The penetrative and phallic elements here are obvious, but also read neutrally in a recurring tension between eroticism and form — shapes and tonal values outweigh anything provocative.

Two lasers and a compact size make it ideal for home studios and pop-up event markets.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's already a lot of competition among the best laser cutters and engravers for crafters, and Creality makes the best budget pick in our guide with its Falcon A1. Today, it's thrown a new contender into the mix, and it looks like it could be a game changer for small personalisation businesses and crafters who want to work remotely.

The next-gen Creality Falcon T1C promises high-performance customisation capabilities, but it's also impressively compact, making it versatile and convenient for things like making custom gifts or adding names, photos, custom text or unique designs to everyday products on location at craft markets and other events (also see our guide to the best 3D printers).

The Falcon T1C is built has a dual-laser configuration that makes it compatible with a wide range of materials. A 15W blue diode laser can process wood, bamboo, leather and dark acrylic, while a 5.5W infrared laser is designed for precision metal marking, dark acrylics and a range of synthetic materials.

Creality says the machine's galvanometer setup (the system that uses motorised mirrors to steer a laser beam) is capable of very fast scan speeds of up to 6,500 mm/s in specified image engraving modes. Using the company's PixelFlow control technology, the system coordinates galvo movement and laser power to preserve fine grayscale details while boosting image-processing efficiency by up to 8x compared to conventional processing under laboratory conditions.

Ultra-fine laser spot sizes (as small as 0.06 x 0.05 mm for the blue diode and 0.03 x 0.03 mm for the infrared laser) promise accurate reproduction for delicate lines, including intricate textures and tiny text, making it possible to personalise very small items.

Aside from the focus on precision, In think what really makes the Falcon T1C a potential game changer is its compact footprint. This makes it an appealing choice for small home studios and workshops but also for anyone who wants to take their customisation business on the move to pop-up event markets. This compactness doesn't necessarily mean sacrificing on potential project size either. The standard 120 x 120 mm working area can be expanded to 120 x 480mm with an optional extension bed for larger items.

One-touch autofocus and camera-assisted positioning should be helpful for speeding up workflows, while the Falcon Design Space software's preset layers eliminate the need to physically swap laser modules or re-align positions, again increasing efficiency for working remotely. It also provides AI Outline Tracing, AI Background Removal, Smart Fill, and AI Filters—to quickly transform design concepts into production-ready physical goods.

#9200. Fujifilm Will Host an X Summit in Paris on December 2

Fujifilm Will Host an X Summit in Paris on December 2

Fujifilm has announced that it will host an X Summit in Paris on December 2 at 4 AM EST. X Summits have traditionally been Fujifilm’s stage for announcing a new product, and given Fujifilm has not released an X-series camera this year, it could very much use one.

“2026 is said to mark 200 years since the invention of photography in France,” Fujifilm says. “To celebrate two centuries of photographic history, and to honor all the photographers and photography lovers who have created countless inspiring images along the way, the next X Summit comes to you from Paris, France.”

Fujifilm has not hosted an X Summit in 2026, although it has hosted multiple Fujikina events around the world, including in Denmark and Poland this past spring and in New York City in October. The last X Summit was held in Shanghai in June 2025, which saw the announcement of the X-E5 and 23mm f/2.8 R. Before that, the X Summit in Prague launched the GFX100RF.

Going 18 months between X Summits is extremely unusual, but getting one in 2026 at all feels like a gift, given how quiet Fujifilm has been this year.

There is no official word on what to expect out of this X Summit (of course), although the perception has been that Fujifilm’s flagship cameras are in dire need of a refresh: the X-Pro, X-T, and X-H cameras are long in the tooth now.

A new camera launch would also be an opportunity to address the largest complaint Fujifilm has come up against: autofocus. To its credit, Fujifilm knows it’s a place it must improve.

“We’re trying,” Yuji Igarashi, General Manager of Professional Imaging Group, Imaging Solutions Division, Fujifilm Corporation, explained to PetaPixel at CP+ 2026 in Yokohama. “We still believe it’s necessary to just continue to improve by algorithm improvement. And it’s not that we’re not doing it. We are continuing to work on it.”

Speaking of future devices, Igarashi said improved sensors and processors likely would help.

“In theory, future devices will be much more advanced, with the consideration of higher processing speed. That would help us as well, but that wouldn’t help existing users, so we’re trying to do both — algorithm improvement plus device improvement.”

Fujifilm will broadcast the X Summit live on its YouTube channel on December 2 at 4 AM EST.

#9199. Shahzia Sikander Confronts British Colonial Legacy in High Line Video Work

With work by Shahzia Sikander and Hylozoic/Desires, “Between Salt and Smoke” simultaneously probes and defies the violent and extractive legacies of British imperialism across Asia.

A new joint video exhibition has opened above 14th Street on the High Line, featuring three moving-image works that illustratively dissect and defy the economic legacies of the British Empire's grip on South Asia and China. Screening daily until January 11, Between Salt and Smoke presents two animated videos by Pakistani-American artist Shahzia Sikander and one documented performance by artists Himali Singh Soin and David Soin Tappeser, who make up the duo Hylozoic/Desires.

The artists examine British colonial extraction and violence in Asia through the lens of the East India Company's monopolies on salt, opium, and other highly valued goods. A new work by Sikander, “3 to 12 Nautical Miles” (2026), consists of hand-painted images that the artist digitally animated in a research-driven cinematic exploration of trade history between the declining Mughal Empire, the East India Company, and the Qing Dynasty.

The most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:

Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:

The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

National income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

Income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

The FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

The lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

Use these calculators to see where you stand on your FI journey.

Find out how much you need to reach financial independence.

Your savings rate matters more than returns. See where you are.

Whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

Multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, New York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

The Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

Pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.
