#9162. Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby’s, Selling for $190.4 M.

After a week dominated by a Nazi-era restitution dispute, Sotheby’s finally got to sell a $180 million Vincent van Gogh painting on Wednesday night—for more than it bargained for.

Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), a picture of chestnut trees in bloom painted just weeks before the artist’s death, sold for $190.4 million (including fees), setting a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The painting, which carried an undisclosed guarantee, hammered at $165 million against an expectation of around $180 million (pre-sale estimates do not include buyer’s fees). Related Articles Amid Legal Controversy, Christie's Withdraws Frida Kahlo Painting Hours Before Auction Sotheby's, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale

After the sale, Kelly Crow reported in the Wall Street Journal that dealer William Acquavella was the painting’s buyer, something that ARTnews also independently confirmed.

The fifth item and cover lot for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” hung behind the rostrum presided over by auctioneer Oliver Barker.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Verger avec cyprès (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold, hammering for $102 million.

Wednesday’s result beats that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

The record is certainly a victory for Sotheby’s, which almost wasn’t going to be able to sell Châtaigniers en fleurs. Last Thursday, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement this week, clearing the painting’s title before the sale. The terms weren’t disclosed, so it’s unclear whether the heirs will receive a share of the proceeds.

For a little perspective, van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) fetched $82.5 million at Christie’s in 1990, then the highest price ever paid for a work of art at auction. That remained the artist’s auction record for 32 years, until the Allen sale. Now, just four years later, the ceiling has moved again.

Painted shortly after van Gogh arrived to Auvers-sur-Oise, Châtaigniers en fleurs is one of only roughly 50 landscapes the artist made during his two-month stay their before his death. Of those, the majority belong to museums, while only an estimated eight are still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

This electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades, last being exhibited at the Guggenheim in 1964. The consignors, Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier, bought it in 1975 and kept it hidden for half a century. That kind of provenance and scarcity is exactly what fuels the trophy market for works of this caliber.

A record of this size for a Post-Impressionist painting might suggest that the market for this category is roaring back. While the market has certainly improved, the rise in sales of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art by 47 percent in 2025 to $1.8 billion, according to the Art Basel and UBS Art Market Report, is still nearly $1 billion short of its $2.6 billion peak in 2022.

#9161. Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

Visitors to the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach interact with a sculpture by the collective MSCHF on the Perrotin stand Photo: Liliana Mora

As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

In a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Oorganisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

“We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” says misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

The campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto says, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

Those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

And yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

“Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”

According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

“Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch says. She plans to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

Still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

As of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

Beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

For the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

“If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto says, “that would be a huge victory.”

The initiative encourages property owners to lend their vacant spaces for free and offers $2,500 stipends to artists—but they may still need to pay rent

The fair will feature 272 exhibitors across a smaller footprint, with blue-chip galleries dispersed throughout the stands

The public programme includes a sculpture park and videos screened on Frank Gehry’s New World Center

#9160. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

#9158. Cézanne ‘Arlequin’ Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby’s, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist

Paul Cézanne made his name painting apples and mountains. But on Wednesday night, the artist’s somewhat severe picture of a teenager in costume became one of the most expensive Cézannes ever sold at auction, after selling at Sotheby’s New York for $111 million with fees.

Arlequin (1888–90), a colorful painting of a young man in a red-and-black diamond-patterned costume, hit the block at Sotheby’s during its dedicated evening sale for the Blaquier-Arrieta collection. The painting hammered at $99 million. Related Articles Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby's, Selling for $190.4 M. Sotheby's, Blaquier-Arrieta Family Reach Deal With Fischer Heirs, Clearing Way for $180 M. Van Gogh Sale

It failed to beat the previous record of $137.8 million set by La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888–90), which sold at Christie’s in 2022 as part of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen‘s collection. Still, once auctioneer Oliver Barker sold Arlequin tonight, a round of applause followed.

Sotheby’s didn’t publish an estimate for Arlequin prior to the sale, though the painting was expected to bring in around $120 million.

The figure in the painting is Cézanne’s son, Paul, dressed as Harlequin, the mischievous character from Italian commedia dell’arte theater. He wears a pointed hat and an elaborate white collar, and holds a slender baton as he walks across a sharply tilted floor. For someone dressed as a comic character, he looks surprisingly serious.

Cézanne painted the picture in Paris between 1888 and 1890, when he was experimenting with a series of theatrical subjects. There are only four paintings in the group, and Arlequin is the only one still in private hands. The others are in museums, including the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., the Pola Museum of Art in Japan, and the Pushkin Museum in Moscow.

The painting comes with quite a history. It passed through the hands of several of the great dealers of the early modern art market, including Ambroise Vollard and Paul Rosenberg, before become part of Lord Victor Rothschild’s collection during the 1930s. His son, Lord Jacob Rothschild, later inherited it, and in 1975 it was sold through London’s Lefevre Gallery to Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier.

Before leaving for Argentina, the painting appeared in major exhibitions at the Museum of Modern Art in New York in 1929, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1952, and the Tate Gallery in London in 1954. After the Blaquiers bought it, it all but disappeared from public view for half a century.

Sotheby’s had guaranteed the painting before Wednesday’s auction, promising the sellers an undisclosed amount regardless of the outcome. It also secured an irrevocable bid, meaning at least one prospective buyer had committed to bidding before the auction began.

Such arrangements are increasingly common at the top of the art market. According to an analysis by the art-market data firm ARTDAI, just 19 guaranteed Cézanne lots make up 63 percent of the hammer-price value in its database of 640 Cézanne sales. In other words, a small number of exceptionally expensive pictures drive much of the artist’s auction business.

The record-setting Cézanne, La Montagne Sainte-Victoire, hammered at $120 million in 2022, more than twice the price achieved by the artist’s next most expensive auction result, a still life that fetched $60.5 million at Sotheby’s in 1999.

Of course, that auction record doesn’t tell the whole story. A version of Cézanne’s The Card Players was reportedly sold privately to Qatar for around $250 million in 2011, a reminder that some of the biggest deals in the art world never reach a public salesroom.

Arlequin was one of 12 paintings offered from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection on Wednesday, alongside Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which had been expected to fetch around $180 million and ended up selling for $190.4 million.

#9157. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 is a worthy upgrade to its predecessor, cleverly interlinking back and lumbar systems so you're completely supported as you move around in the chair. It's still not the most attractive of chairs, and assembly could be more straightforward, but once it's up and running, you'll find levels of ergonomics that actually belie its $499.99 / £459.99 price.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Chairs seem to come in pairs. I've been getting a lot of chairs in for review recently, with the remarkably similar Secretlab Titan Evo and the DXRacer Martian Pro showing up around the same time. Now, having just reviewed the Boulies EP600, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 has taken my focus – and they have so much in common, it’s like they were separated at birth.

The design of the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 is almost a mirror image of the Boulies EP600: Both feature curvy three-piece back panels with responsive lumbar supports, pull-out footrests, and they’re roughly the same price. But where the Boulies EP600 was feature-packed and poorly executed, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 nails the execution, and it’s definitely one of the best office chairs for back pain. It’s also a marked improvement on its predecessor, the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro.

Like most of Sihoo’s chairs, the Doro C300 Pro makes use of mesh throughout. There’s nothing wrong with that: mesh makes chairs lighter and easier to pack, but it lacks the sink-in sumptuousness of cushioned chairs, including its own budget-friendly Sihoo M18.

However, where the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro gets everything absolutely right is in its engineering. While it can feel a little clunky and firm to start with, once it’s dialled-in it reaches astonishing levels of comfort with the versatility to move around and change positions.

This begins with the lumbar support, which naturally moves and follows your lower back as you lean backwards and forwards. Unlike the aggressive system in the Boulies EP600, it flows with you and never becomes intrusive.

Sihoo also includes a sacral support system here, which cradles the heart-shaped sacrum bone at the base of your spine with a gentle pressure I’ve never felt before. It’s one of the best lumbar systems I’ve used, and it’s adjustable so you can hone it just as you want it.

The lumbar support moves alongside the rest of the chair as you shift around; lean back and the armrests follow the backrest and the seat cushion moves forwards. It's always got your back (literally), and it delivers on the promise that the automated Hbada X7 failed to deliver, and it does so without motors or AI.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Endless adjustments don’t end there: the armrests can also be tweaked and rotated to optimise your comfort levels, apparently through eight dimensions. This sounds like it might break the very fabric of reality, but if I’m going to implode with an alternative-dimension version of myself, at least I can do so with comfortable elbows.

One neat feature here is that the rear portion of the armrests flips up and locks into place, giving you a little more comfort when you’re reading, sketching, or diving back into another 16-hour GTA VI binge, and the (optional) mesh leg rest also helps you relax into a state of utter relaxation as you cause chaos in Vice City.

Sihoo reckons the chair will suit anyone up to 6’ 3”, and it fits my 6’ 4” height perfectly, with the headrest in just the right place. Sihoo has also upgraded the weight accommodation to a maximum of 136 kg, so this is a chair that can be used by pretty much anybody and everybody.

Beren’s take on the original C300 Pro was that it was one ugly motherfu…rniture. The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 doesn’t break the mould in terms of looks, and it’s almost indistinguishable from other ultra-adjustable ergonomic office chairs: it’s the Boulies EP600, it’s the Hinomi H2 Pro.

These chairs tend to be triumphs of function over form, although I’m not sure anyone outside of Gold's Gym will have shoulders wide enough to justify the upper width of the backrest. Where they differentiate themselves is in the view from the back.

The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 looks reasonably attractive: the headrest’s large “eyes” and its nose-like supports actually recall Gonzo a little bit, while the armrests, in grey, have a friendly cetacean look about them. It’s still not the best-looking chair, but these touches add a playfulness that reduces its dour, generic design.

Choosing the grey colourway Sihoo sent us also helps lighten the heaviness of the design and stops it looking like a predatory black blob in front of your desk.

Take note: this is a herculean, 27kg chair that comes in two boxes, and not something you’ll want to be moving vertically once assembled. Within one of those boxes you’ll also find my pet peeve with Sihoo chairs: having to put the base together and insert those 10 screws. I’ve done it countless times and it never gets easier or more fun. It makes me think about my own mortality.

Sihoo’s assembly process is nowhere near as straightforward as, say, Branch’s. There is a fair amount of cross-referencing to be done between the manual, the screw blister-pack, and the chair itself, to the extent that I thought an escape room-style door would open somewhere when I’d completed it. The armrests connect via washers that seem a little too big for their holes, and they take a bit of brute force to get them in place.

Sihoo has kept the number of steps involved to the absolute minimum, and when it’s done it feels remarkably sturdy. But the niggling annoyances in its construction do add up, and it feels like there are plenty of opportunities for Sihoo to simplify things. They can start with that wretched base.

Office chair pricing is so complicated and fluid that it can be hard to find a coherent and consistent price, but apparently the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 carries an RRP of $499.99 / £409.99, with the footrest costing an extra $40 / £50, but these prices are often discounted. The Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V1 was a frankly absurd RRP of $699 when Beren reviewed it; thankfully, Sihoo seems to have made its pricing more sensible since then.

Is it worth it? I’d say a definite yes; despite my grumbles about the construction process, this is a comfortable and innovative chair that gets a lot of things right. If you’re torn between the Sihoo Doro Pro C300 V2 and the Boulies EP600 ($489.99 / £429.99) I’d definitely recommend the Sihoo option.

If your budget stretches a little more, then the Hinomi H2 Pro ($ / £759) is a worthy contender, with similar adjustability and a neat folding feature — although it lacks the Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2’s versatile armrests. And, of course, there’s the ever-dependable Sihoo M18 (under $ / £200), if you want to spend less but still need a decent level of lumbar support.

Sihoo’s upgrades really do make a big difference with the Doro C300 Pro V2. The way it all works together is a marvel of engineering, and it adds up to one of the best back support systems I’ve ever used. The fact that it achieves it without batteries and motors is impressive in itself. It’s a chair that cradles your back from the moment you sit in it, but that can also be tweaked in just the right ways, without ever becoming overwhelming or overcomplicated.

The biggest downsides here are its chunky looks and its fiddly assembly process, but both of these will evaporate the moment you sit on it. It’s the perfect chair for people who like to move around a lot, and who like to kick back for entertainment in the same chair they work in.

#9155. Van Gogh painting sells for record $190m at Sotheby’s following Nazi loot claims

Auctioneer Oliver Barker selling Blossoming Chestnut Trees on Wednesday, 18 November Courtesy Sotheby's

One of Vincent van Gogh’s last paintings, long hidden from public view, sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees) at Sotheby’s New York on Wednesday (18 November), breaking the artist’s auction record. The result helped propel two back-to-back sales to a combined $663.26m ($777.8m with fees), with additional auction records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas.

But the landmark results were high points for an evening of uneven bidding, with just more than one-third of works selling for below their pre-sale estimates. The Blaquier-Arrieta collection, billed as the most valuable collection to come to auction in New York this season, brought in $358m ($412m with fees), falling short of its roughly $450m estimate. Sotheby’s Modern Evening sale, which followed immediately afterwards, generated another $305.21m ($365.8m with fees) against a $260.2m to $378.4m overall estimate.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), the most valuable lot offered across New York’s auction houses this season, had attracted attention even before reaching the rostrum. One of Van Gogh’s final paintings before his death in 1890, the work had for decades been out of public view in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, built by Argentine sugar industry heiress Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, who served as president of Argentina’s largest sugar producer. Just a day before the sale, Sotheby’s announced that a settlement had been reached between the Blaquier heirs and the heirs of the painting’s previous owners, Hedwig and Samuel Fischer, following questions about the work’s Nazi-era provenance.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) sold for $165m ($190.4m with fees). Courtesy Sotheby's

Estimated to fetch around $180m, the painting hammered at $165m ($190.4m with fees) after nearly five minutes of bidding, eventually going to a bidder in the room—William Aquavella, the head of Acquavella Galleries. Despite the hammer price falling short of its estimate, the Sotheby’s-guaranteed work surpassed Van Gogh’s previous auction record of $117m with fees, set in 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888) sold at Christie’s Paul Allen sale. The result also made it the second most valuable object ever sold at Sotheby’s, behind Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which fetched $236.4m with fees during last November’s marquee sales, and the fourth most valuable painting ever sold at auction.

Soon afterwards, Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888-90) came to the rostrum. The painting, the last of the artist’s four works from the series still in public hands, hammered at $99m ($111m with fees), falling short of its $120m estimate. It also failed to surpass Cézanne’s auction record, set during the same 2022 Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York, when the landscape La Montagne Sainte-Victoire (1888-90) fetched $138m with fees. Nevertheless, Arlequin became the most valuable Cézanne painting from the Harlequin series to sell at auction.

Ultimately, six of the collection’s 12 lots hammered below their low estimates, while five sold within or at their estimate ranges. Just one work exceeded expectations: the final lot, Camille Pissarro’s Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875), which hammered at $1.62m ($2m with fees), against a $700,000 to $900,000 estimate.

The subsequent Modern Evening sale generated $305.21m ($365.8m with fees), although bidding was similarly patchy. Of the works sold, 14 hammered below their low estimates, 21 sold within their estimate ranges and 11 exceeded their high estimates.

The top lot was René Magritte’s L’Ami de l’ordre (1964), which hammered at $39m ($45.5m with fees), far surpassing its $25m to $35m estimate. Combining the artist’s signature bowler-hatted figure with a nighttime landscape, the painting was consigned by the estate of beauty pioneer Sydell Miller. Two years ago, 25 works from her collection brought in $215.9m with fees during a single-owner auction at Sotheby’s November marquee sales. According to Sotheby’s, only one related composition now remains in private hands. L’Ami de l’ordre is the most valuable Magritte painting featuring a bowler hat to sell at auction.

Harriet Tubman (1931) by Aaron Douglas. Courtesy Sotheby's

One of the evening’s most exciting results came courtesy of the Harlem Renaissance artist Aaron Douglas, whose Harriet Tubman (1931) shattered his previous auction record. The painting depicts the American abolitionist with her arms raised overhead, breaking a chain amid a leafy landscape and a smoking cannon. Estimated at $2.5m to $3.5m, it hammered at $12m ($14.48m with fees) after a seven-minute bidding battle. At one point, the competition pitted father and daughter against each other on the telephones, bidding on behalf of their respective clients: George Wachter, Sotheby’s chairman of the Americas, and Jacqueline Wachter, vice-chairman of private sales for contemporary art and head of the Los Angeles office. The result far surpassed Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set at Swann in 2008. Proceeds from the sale will benefit Bennett College, one of just two historically Black women’s colleges in the US.

Mary Cassatt also established a new auction record when Summertime (1894–95) hammered at $11m ($13.3m with fees) to an online bidder, exceeding its $7m to $10m estimate. The result surpassed her previous record of $7.49m, set at Christie’s New York in 2022. The painting came from the collection of the late oil tycoon Armand Hammer, with proceeds benefiting his eponymous foundation.

Only one lot failed to sell: Remedios Varo’s El vagabundo, which passed at $1.5m. Three other works, by Henri Matisse, Cézanne and Magritte, were withdrawn during the sale. Together, the withdrawn lots carried estimates totalling between $12.5m and $18.5m.

#9154. A Tiny Monet With a Wild Backstory Just Fetched More Than 20 Times its Estimate at a Christie’s Day Sale

The auction houses’ marquee evening sales get all the headlines, with high-eight-figure artworks and high-nine-figure totals, sometimes approaching the billion-dollar mark when the market is flush.

But the more modest daytime sales of lower-priced materials occasionally contain real treasures. When I wrote about them for Artnet News in 2015, experts told me that this is where the houses make a lot of their profits; dealers haunt these sales to stock up on inventory; they are far less stage-managed than the evening events; they may be more indicative of the actual health of the market; and you can find better deals. Related Articles Christie's Buzzy 20th-Century Sale Totals $626.6 M., with Starry Lots Above $80 M. by Kandinsky and Klimt Seven Works Reportedly from Jeff Koons's Collection Fetch a Lackluster $104 M. at Christie's, Led by a $31.2 M. Picasso

And they can occasionally spark serious bidding wars. On Wednesday, a tiny artwork by a titan of French Impressionism became the latest example.

Claude Monet’s La Barque (ca. 1874), which came under the hammer at Christie’s Rockefeller Center saleroom at a day sale of Impressionist and modern art, was estimated at $300,000 to $500,000, but fetched just shy of $7 million. Its modest estimate matched its diminutive size: it measures only 2¾ by 3½ inches, so it sold for $722,285.71 per square inch.

More than 20 bidders fought for the tiny panel, some in the room and some bidding on the phone via Christie’s specialists, says the house; the contest went on for six minutes and 45 seconds, and Rachel White Young, head of the 20th-century evening sale, won the prize for her client.

Even before making a little auction history on Wednesday, the painting had an unusual backstory.

Paris art dealer Georges Petit, a collector and supporter of the Impressionists, commissioned it from the artist; the magazine L’Art Moderne wrote about it in June 1902, relating how the collector carried around small pieces of wood, cut to identical sizes, which he handed out to artists he admired. He would offer them 100 francs and ask if they would return the petite panel as a painting. He did the same with Camille Corot, Édouard Manet, Camille Pissarro, and Pierre-Auguste Renoir, all of whom obliged.

All five would come into the collection of Thérèse and Frédéric Humbert, notorious figures in French high society. She claimed to have been willed a fortune by an imaginary American millionaire, Robert Crawford, whose life she had supposedly saved. They borrowed against an imaginary fortune, buying a grand home and occupying the center of Parisian social life for two decades, until bank officials started asking questions and her creditors sued and the tissue of lies was shredded.

Funny enough, the resulting sale of their possessions would take place in 1902 at none other than Galerie Georges Petit. Galerie Bernheim-Jeune bought it and it remained with that family until 2013, when the ollectors Marlene and Spencer Hays got it at Paris auction house Hôtel Drouot, for the hammer price of €200,000. They began selling books door-to-door as a summer job for Southwestern Company and later went on to run the busines and start a clothing company.

According to their foundation, when asked what was the most fun part of their lives, they would say, “learning about art and building a collection that we treasure,” but would also quote Sir Richard Attenborough to the effect that art collectors are “simply its temporary, fortunate and delighted custodians.” Their collection included works by Pierre Bonnard, Edgar Degas, Henri Matisse, Amedeo Modigliani, and Édouard Vuillard.

They were as good as their word; they granted their collection to Paris’s Musée d’Orsay in 2016. It was the largest foreign collection donated since World War II, with some 600 masterworks from the late 19th and early 20th centuries. He died the next year, survived by Marlene.

Is it a step too far for virtual branding?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The best NHL logos are timeless, but the National Hockey League has been covering them up recently, at least on television broadcasts. After the addition of dynamic digital advertising on dashers and on the ice, the league's latest technological 'advance' is the use of digital overlays to replace real centre logos with temporary virtual ones.

Spectators in the arena see the home team's usual design, but viewers watching on TV are shown the team's Hometown Remix logo, a temporary alternate design being used for select games. It must have seemed like a great idea when it was floated, but it doesn't seem to be going down well with viewers, with some saying they'll stop watching if the practice continues.

@The_Mexinadian There’s already too much virtual crap on the ice and video as it is. Why do we need a HUGE fake logo that hurts my eyes whenever anyone skates over it?!November 15, 2026

Hometown Remix is a leaguewide campaign in which each team has a special-edition uniform featuring specifically local references. Many teams are using modified, throwback or entirely redesigned logos. The NHL says the campaign "uniquely and authentically celebrates the fans, fabric, and local culture of each NHL team and the cities they call home".

But in sports like the NHL, a logo design isn't just an identity, it's revenue. Multiple logos, throwback designs and temporary remixes all largely about selling a new range of merchandise. Putting a temporary logo on the ice becomes highly visible advertising for alternate jerseys. The problem is that it's appalling to look at.

The ice is *the* thing that immediately separates watching hockey from watching any other sport the instant you turn it on. It's beautiful and unique. Slapping giant fake digital novelty logos on top of the earnestly painted logos that are actually there is a shame. https://t.co/JvoXxCJWkONovember 13, 2026

You can literally see a white glow around every player at center ice??? How was this approvedNovember 18, 2026

WHAT IS THE POINT!?!?! https://t.co/GLRkQI5M30November 15, 2026

Some viewers already complained about the digitisation of adverts on dashers and on the ice to make them look more prominent. For some, the new virtual logos is the last straw, making the viewing experience feel detached from reality.

The lack of motion blur or shadows on the digital fake when players pass over the centre of the ice makes it look uncanny, as though players are passing in front of a badly keyed green screen. Any black in the design can make the puck momentarily disappear from view.

"When they brought in the digitally superimposed ads on the boards I stopped watching altogether. Too distracting and horribly done. I remember seeing players disappear into the ads," one person writes on X.

Some fans are concerned that the NHL's use of virtual team logos could be merely the start and that the league might be testing the ground to potentially replace team logos with sponsors. I'm not sure brands would want to be associated with the backlash that would cause.

Designers have to consider an increasingly wide range of potential digital applications for logo designs these days. On the ice in an NHL game probably shouldn't be one of them.

Feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

How you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

The resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date]."

The transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the company, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice says never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

If you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

Health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:

COBRA: Continues your employer plan for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?"

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

Pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the issue your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

Before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

Pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream company in three years.

At minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

#9150. Led by Record-Breaking $190.4 M. van Gogh, Sotheby’s Impressionist and Modern Art Sales Rake in $777.8 M.

By Daniel Cassady, Sarah Douglas November 19, 2026 12:13am

It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York tonight brought in a total of $777.8 million.

That total is the highest one for a single night at the auction house, edging past the $706 million achieved last November at the house’s inaugural evening double-header at the Breuer building. And while the 12 lots from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection came in at $412 million, just shy of their presale low estimate of $414.5 million, those dozen works still managed to set a record for a single-owner evening sale dedicated to Impressionist and modern art at Sotheby’s. (Unless otherwise noted, prices cited here are inclusive of fees.) Related Articles Cézanne 'Arlequin' Sells for $111 M. at Sotheby's, Becoming One of the Most Expensive Paintings by the Artist Van Gogh Slashes Auction Record at Sotheby's, Selling for $190.4 M.

Two lots in the Blaquier-Arrieta collection were the most anticipated paintings of the season: Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890) and Paul Cézanne’s Arlequin (1888–90).

They both achieved eye-popping prices—$190.4 million for the van Gogh, the artist’s highest price to date and the highest price for any work of art ever sold at Sotheby’s, and $111 million for the Cézanne, the second-highest price for Cézanne at auction. But the bidding was anticlimactic.

Both works hammered below their pre-sale estimates. There was just a smattering of bids on the van Gogh. The Cézanne inched along with four bids alternating between Sotheby’s specialists Lisa Dennison, Chairman Americas, and Helena Newman, chairman of Sotheby’s Europe. It hammered to Newman.

Asked after the sale whether the publicity surrounding the restitution claim against the van Gogh had affected bidding, Sotheby’s CEO Charles Stewart said he didn’t think so.

“First of all, it’s a record price for the artist,” he said, pointing out that it was also the fourth-highest price achieved by any artist at auction. “I think you have to separate auction heat from auction results,” he said.

The liveliest bidding came for the final two paintings, both of them with estimates on the lower side, for this sale. Edith Eustis and Simon Stark on the phones, as well as several bidders in the room, went for Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec’s Femme assise de profil vers la gauche (1890). It sold to a man in the second row for $3.8 million. Then, Wendy Lin, Serena Hildebrandt, and Alina Davey battled on the phones for the Camille Pissarro landscape, Maison de Piette à Montfoucault, effet de neige, avec un homme portant un fagot (1875). It came down to Lin and Davey, and went to Davey for $2 million. It was bought by the same bidder who bought Edgar Degas’s Avant la course (ca. 1893) for $18 million a few lots earlier, bidding with Sotheby’s Ben Doller.

Things picked up considerably during the 47-lot, multiple-owner sale that followed, which saw lively bidding in the room and no fewer than 33 Sotheby’s specialists fielding bids over the phones. All told, this sale made $365.8 million, with all but one of the lots sold. It helped that the highest-priced lots came early in the sale and generated heated bidding wars.

The top price from that sale was the $47.3 million for Edward Hopper’s 1944 seascape The Martha Mckeen of Wellfleet, from the collection of Baroness Carmen Thyssen-Bornemisza. It’s far from Hopper’s record—$91.8 million for Chop Suey from the Barney Ebsworth collection at Christie’s in November 2018—but it is his second-highest price at auction. As dealer Lock Kresler pointed out on the Nota Bene podcast, the closest comparison is another Hopper seascape, Blackwell’s Island, from 1928, which sold at Christie’s in 2013 for $19.1 million.

The Martha Mckeen sparked a bidding war between four Sotheby’s specialists on the phone bank, with Scott Niichel, vice chairman and head of middle market for modern and contemporary art, coming out the winner. Accounting for fees, the work made $47.8 million.

Close behind the Hopper was the $45 million achieved by Rene Magritte’s 1964 painting L’Ami de l’ordre, which stars the painter’s famous man in a bowler hat. It came from the collection of Sydell Miller, who bought it in 1998 for a mere $5.3 million. The previous record for a bowler hat painting was for the one sold at Christie’s London in March 2024 for £33.7 million (about $43.2 million), Magritte’s third-highest price. Several bidders in the room went up against two Sotheby’s specialists, Jackie Wachter and Bame Fierro March. A bidder in the room was the winner, but no one seemed to be able to identify him.

Also adding sparks early in the sale was Aaron Douglas’s 1931 painting of Harriet Tubman. Even if it had merely sold near its pre-sale estimate of $2.5 million–$3.5 million, the piece would have handily broken the record for Douglas: $600,000, for a piece sold at Swann Galleries auction house in 2008. But it more than quadrupled that estimate to make $14.1 million, all of which will go to Bennett College, a historically Black women’s college, that sold the piece.

Some eight bidders went after the painting, beginning with Jackie Wachter going up against her father, George Wachter, who serves as Sotheby’s chairman of North America and South America. Several bidders in the room popped in before Sotheby’s head of American art Stefany Morris entered the war. In the end, it was Morris versus the room, with Morris the winner.

“We knew it was going to make a big price,” Sotheby’s vice chairman and head of contemporary art David Galperin said after the sale. “That’s one of the most exciting auction moments—when you have something that is so categorically the very best” by an artist whose work rarely comes to auction.

Halfway through the sale came another big moment: a painting by Mary Cassatt, Summertime (1894–95), from the Armand Hammer collection, sold for $13.3 million, a new record that nearly doubles the previous one, $7.5 million. Here the evening’s depth of bidding was again on display: specialists David Galperin, Caroline Seabolt, Lin, and Simon Stock all went after it, but the winner was an online bidder.

On the lower end of the price spectrum, a landscape by Chaim Soutine, Place à Céret (1921–22), estimated at just $800,000–$1.2 million, made $3.9 million. Five Sotheby’s specialists on the phones wanted the picture; so did bidders in the room. Jen Hua, deputy chairman of Sotheby’s Asia, cast the final bid.

Over the course of the evening, Hua and Lin, the Sotheby’s Asia chairman, were especially busy. Asian collectors bought works by Signac, Maurice de Vlaminck, Cézanne, Claude Monet, Renoir, Soutine, Egon Schiele, and Degas (including the Degas in the Blaquier-Arrieta sale for $18 million). They bid on works by Monet (the Blaquier-Arrieta picture that sold for $20.2 million), Picasso, Magritte, Cassatt, and Degas.

The sale was not without hitches. A Remedios Varo drawing failed to sell, and three lots—pieces by Magritte, Cézanne, and Matisse—were apparently withdrawn while the sale was in progress, given that the withdrawals were not announced prior to the sale, as is customary. (Two of the withdrawn lots–Henri Matisse’s La Jetée à Collioure (estimate $5–$7 million), and Paul Cézanne’s L’Oncle Dominique (estimate $3–$5 million)–are among the 11 in the sale that come from the collection of George Weiss, the hedge fund founder now in bankruptcy, as ARTnews revealed earlier this month.)

Every one of the Blaquier lots was guaranteed. For Phillip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, that brought up a question about Sotheby’s strategy.

“The guarantees were just too high,” he told ARTnews immediately after the Blaquier-Arrieta sale. “I think these guarantees are just pushing the limit.”

He said Sotheby’s had left buyers very little room to compete, and had been too confident in its pricing, with the result a string of lots that attracted little meaningful competition.

Calling it “a little bit of overconfidence” on the house’s part, he speculated that they might have lost as much as $50 million on guarantees.

Stewart, the Sotheby’s CEO, defended the house’s approach to the evening.

“Our estimates weren’t shy,” he acknowledged. “You can read into that whatever you like. We were happy with the result of everything.”

#9149. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.
