The Musso E80 Muse is a chair built with women in mind, and it shows. Designed to fit anyone from 4ft 9 to 5ft 11, it solved problems I didn’t realise I had. The soft, silky materials feel a world away from the usual brutalist office chair, and the lumbar support is the best I’ve tried: my lower back ache disappeared after a few days. The levers and knobs feel a bit plasticky, and it took a while to find my perfect position, but once I got there – wow. Well worth trying if you’re on the smaller side.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

As most people know, most products are tested on men. From pharmaceuticals to seatbelts, women’s bodies are rarely taken into account in product creation. I’ll admit I’d never considered that my office chair feels just a bit too big for me (and it's got slightly the wrong proportions), but it’s true. Unlike the pink Biro (remember that?), an office chair is a case where a woman’s version could genuinely be considered, so I was happy to try the Musso E80 Muse. Is this heading for our best office chair for back pain guide?

The chair has been built with women in mind in a host of ways, from its size and proportions (it’s designed to fit anyone from 4ft 9 to 5ft 11 – I'm 5 ft 5, fyi) to its materials. With all that in mind, it’s almost great. It has a couple of compromises at this price point, but I think they're worth making.

Want a chair at a discount price? See our Black Friday office chair deals page.

The Muse comes in soft colours: Blush, Pink, Grey and White. It’s a palette removed from the usual office chair offerings, and I won’t comment on the ‘girls like pink’ association. It’s nice to have something that looks more in keeping with my office than the brutalist chairs I’ve had before. The materials are silky smooth and soft, which is pretty delightful.

I’m not saying men wouldn’t want a chair made of something more comfortable and plush than the standard mesh of an ergonomic chair, but sitting on this one was a lightbulb moment. Other upgrades include the flex when you lean back, a handy adjustable footstool, and a much softer, more adjustable lumbar support than on any chair I’ve tried before.

As mentioned, the proportions are different – it has a shorter backrest and the chair can go down further for shorter legs. All of this is fully adjustable so, in theory, you can find the perfect fit.

So that’s the positives for design. The minus points go to some of the other material aspects. The levers and knobs feel brittle and plasticky when you adjust them, which makes me wonder if they could have been sturdier, made from slightly more premium materials. At this price point, I can see they’ve put the money into the other materials, which is understandable.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

I’ll start by saying that at first I wasn’t convinced. It took me a long time to adjust the chair into the perfect position and I didn’t think I’d get there. But let me tell you, once I did – wow.

The chair has a lot more ‘give’ than others I’ve tried, allowing you to move around, and I feel much more supported, especially by the lumbar support. It took a while to get into position, but I feel its benefit more than with any other chair. I didn’t realise how supported my lower back could feel. I’m not giving a medical opinion, but my lower back ache disappeared after a few days in the Muse, which was a big surprise.

Let’s discuss seat height. Until I lowered this chair all the way down, I had NO IDEA how I could be sitting. My legs usually dangle, so I put them on a block, but being able to drop the seat all the way and then move it back and forward for the perfect support was a revelation.

This could also be the first time my head has felt supported: I can finally move the headrest all the way forward to meet my head.

The soft materials make a huge difference to how it feels to sit in the chair. It feels like the chair is rising up to support me, rather than the hard, unyielding feeling I didn’t realise my old chair was giving me.

At $369, this chair sits at the lower end of mid-range. It's an accessible price point, and it delivers a lot of benefit for certain people at this price. To keep it accessible, and to focus on the things that matter, Musso has compromised on some of the materials (levers, the finish of some of the plastic parts), but the materials that matter – the seat, arms, lumbar support pad and soft mesh, have lovely attention to detail. I think it's priced about right when you see what else is on the market.

If you have always found office chairs to be unforgiving, slightly the wrong size and shape, and unsightly then this could be a good option for you. Of course, you don't have to be a woman to enjoy these benefits, so if you fall into the height range I'd give it a go.

#9130. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#9129. AT-LARS’ adaptable museum combines scaffolding and translucent facade in indonesia

bridging pavilion and infrastructure, the modular form prioritizes reuse and adaptability over the fixed permanence of conventional museum architecture.

AT-LARS edited by christina vergopoulou November 18, 2026 4 min

Completed in 2024 at the Pertamina Mandalika International Circuit in Indonesia, the Pertamina MotoGP Experience Gallery is a 1,400-sqm, two-story cultural pavilion designed and constructed in four months by AT-LARS. Built to operate over a multi-year lifecycle, the structure employs a modular scaffolding system as both its primary load-bearing framework and architectural expression. Echoing the industrial aesthetic of the adjacent circuit grandstands, this demountable construction method minimizes on-site labor and material waste while allowing the building to be reconfigured, expanded, or relocated. Bridging pavilion and infrastructure, this modular form prioritizes reuse and adaptability over the fixed permanence of conventional museum architecture.

The design studio organizes the massing around the ‘Speed Box,’ an elongated upper volume split into two parallel gallery wings separated by a central open-air foyer and circulation spine. Elevated above a ground-level base containing retail, administrative offices, and storage, the two upper volumes are linked by elevated walkways, gathering terraces, and circuit viewing platforms, with elongated ramps along the east and west facades providing continuous accessible circulation between levels. Programmatically, the South Gallery operates as a flexible hall for launches and community events, while the North Gallery serves as Indonesia’s first official Mandalika MotoGP™ Gallery, housing motorsport memorabilia and installations.

Wrapping the steel framework, translucent, lightly tinted prefabricated polycarbonate panels are arranged in horizontal bands to diffuse daylight into the interiors and allow the structure to illuminate from within after dark. By pairing this panelized envelope with a reusable scaffolding skeleton, the pavilion establishes a low-waste construction model suited for fast-paced motorsport and event environments.

architect: AT-LARS | @atelierlarassati lead architect: Stephanie Larassati

design team: Raihan HJP, Angelika location: Lombok, Indonesia

#9128. BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

#9126. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9124. Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

#9123. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

Last medically reviewed on June 30, 2024

#9122. translucent Y2K electronics inspire iridescent skin of cadillac’s F1 race car

cadillac wraps its MAC-26 in iridescent circuitry graphics inspired by translucent electronics for the 2026 las vegas grand prix.

The Cadillac Formula 1 Team has unveiled a translucent-look livery for its MAC-26 race car ahead of the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix. Inspired by the illuminated streets of the Las Vegas Strip, the design covers sections of the car’s familiar black-and-white bodywork with a web of iridescent circuitry. Pink and violet lines spread across the nose and sidepods to give the impression that the car’s electronic components are glowing beneath a transparent shell.

The effect is created through layered graphics applied to the car’s bodywork. From certain angles, the colored lines appear suspended beneath the surface, while soft washes of blue and purple give the finish a sense of depth. The Cadillac team will debut the design during its final American race of the season, when the cars take to the Strip Circuit under the city’s lights.

The livery of the Cadillac F1 race car brings to mind the translucent consumer electronics of the late 1990s and early 2000s, when computers and gaming accessories arrived with colorful plastic casings that revealed their internal workings. The team at Cadillac takes a similar visual approach, with fine lines resembling a circuit board running across a glassy, iridescent surface. The familiar mechanical silhouette of the Formula 1 car becomes the canvas for a graphic treatment that suggests something happening beneath its outer skin.

The design becomes especially intricate around the cockpit and engine cover, where branching lines overlap in shades of electric pink and blue. The front wing carries a softer version of the same pattern. Against the surrounding black carbon-fiber elements and white bodywork, the colorful detailing gives the MAC-26 an almost computer-generated appearance.

Beyond its Las Vegas inspiration, the circuitry is a visual reference to the work involved in establishing Cadillac’s Formula 1 operation. The team describes the livery as a tribute to the people and engineering efforts behind its debut season, which has seen an entirely new American team enter the championship. The intersecting lines suggest the complex network of systems required to bring a Formula 1 car to the grid.

This idea comes through most clearly in the close-up renderings, where the colorful pathways appear to run through the body of the car itself. The graphics play with transparency while preserving the streamlined form and aerodynamic components of the MAC-26. The effect is particularly striking across the broad white surfaces, where the circuitry stands out against the darker mechanical elements.

The Las Vegas design completes a series of special liveries introduced throughout Cadillac’s inaugural Formula 1 season. The team first revealed its asymmetrical black-and-white identity during a Super Bowl commercial in February 2026, before introducing an American-inspired design in Miami. A red, white, and blue edition followed at Silverstone for the Fourth of July, while Austin brought another variation on the team’s American identity.

For its fourth and final special livery of the year, Cadillac turns to the lights of Las Vegas and the technology behind its new racing operation. Drivers Sergio Pérez and Valtteri Bottas will bring the design to the Las Vegas Grand Prix on November 21, where the circuitry will be seen in motion against the illuminated city skyline. After the race, the cars will return to their regular black-and-white livery for the remaining rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

The best 3D scanners have changed the game for custom manufacturing, and they continue to advance. Creality, which also makes some of the best 3D printers, already has a wide range of solutions, including the versatile Sermoon P1S.

Now, it's added to the family a new device that looks set up to speed up workflows for those working in automobile custromisation. The Raptor Pro Max builds on the existing Raptor Pro handheld scanner but almost doubles the number of cross blue laser lines and unlocks a 40% larger single capture range.

The Raptor Pro Max has 42 cross blue laser lines, up from 22 on the Raptor Pro, and it can reach up to 1.26 million measurements, raising the maximum scanning rate by approximately 91% while offering a single capture range of up to 480 × 330 mm at a working distance of 550 mm.

That wider coverage and higher scanning rate mean that you can capture more of a bumper, door or body panel in each pass, which gives successive frames more shared geometry to maintain stable tracking. The expanded coverage also helps reduce the number of markers required by up to 25%.

Creality says the reduction of repeat passes, the need for repositioning and the application of markers means users can complete scans of automotive workpieces in up to 40% less time. That will allow custom parts to be moved into design and trial-fitting work more quickly.

For smaller features, there's also the option to switch to seven parallel blue laser lines to capture edges, threads, and chamfers. Together, the two blue laser modes cover objects from 5 to 4,000 mm in size. Creality cites volumetric accuracy of 0.02 mm + 0.08 mm/m.² The blue lasers can also capture suitable black and metallic surfaces without scanning spray.

During handheld scanning, real-time preview in Creality Scan lets operators monitor coverage as they move around a part. The Blue Laser Line Mode operates at up to 60 fps and the a near-infrared (NIR) structured-light mode at up to 30 fps, with geometry or texture tracking. There's built-in anti-shake functionality to help reduce the impact of hand movement.

#9120. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

#9119. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#9118. First Ferrari Style flagship store in New York features metallic facade

Photography courtesy Ferrari Style

Architecture studios Gonzalez Haase AAS and Formafantasma have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

Under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.

A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.

It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.

Wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.

Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.

Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

#9117. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#9116. BIG stacks timber volumes with alpine views for new neighborhood in switzerland

bjarke ingels group proposes four timber buildings in thun, switzerland with stepped hotel terraces overlooking the alps.

Bjarke Ingels Group / BIG unveils plans for four timber buildings in Thun, Switzerland, where the architecture firm will help shape the entrance to the city’s emerging Siegenthalergut district. The 13,000-square-meter development brings together two hotels and residential buildings, with stacked wooden volumes that project outward above the street. Set against the Bernese Alps, the architecture is defined by deep window grids and large terraces carved into the buildings’ stepped facades.

The proposal, developed with landscape architects August + Margrith Künzel, was selected through a competition organized by Frutiger AG and the city of Thun. Titled Nachwachsende Stadt, or Growing City, the scheme occupies one of the first two plots planned for the new neighborhood. The site sits opposite a sports center and the future headquarters of the Swiss Football Association to give the BIG-designed buildings a prominent position along the city’s western entrance.

At the southwest corner of the site, the team at BIG brings a three-star and a four-star hotel together under one roof. Shared amenity spaces cut diagonally through the structure, creating a series of setbacks that interrupt its otherwise regular timber grid. These shifts make room for outdoor terraces overlooking the neighboring sports facilities, with the Bernese Alps rising in the distance. A restaurant at the top of the building will give guests an even broader view of the surrounding landscape.

At street level, a cantilevered corner marks the main hotel entrance, opening onto a drop-off plaza beneath the projecting upper floors. Commercial spaces line the adjacent boulevard, bringing activity to the building’s ground floor. Across the facade, large square windows sit within deeply framed timber modules, while recessed portions reveal warmer, sheltered spaces behind the exterior grid. The alternating volumes give the hotel a sculptural profile that changes depending on where it is viewed from.

To the east, the remaining timber buildings accommodate residences with flexible layouts and projecting bays. Here, the same geometric language takes on a more domestic scale. Balconies extend outward from the facades, while recessed loggias create sheltered outdoor rooms. The shifting arrangement of these openings gives each elevation a different rhythm, with the projecting volumes bringing daylight deeper into the apartments.

The residential buildings face an internal courtyard, where winding paths move through gardens and planted gathering spaces. Renderings picture grassy areas beneath the timber facades, with balconies overlooking the shared landscape. Small plazas and seating areas are distributed throughout the development, connecting the homes to the surrounding neighborhood.

Of the project’s total 13,000 square meters, approximately 6,500 are dedicated to residential uses, alongside 6,000 square meters of hotel space and another 400 square meters for commercial activities.

The use of timber extends across all four buildings, establishing a consistent material language while helping reduce the development’s embodied carbon footprint. BIG has designed the timber elements for future disassembly and reuse, allowing components to be recovered as the buildings change over time. The deep balconies and roof overhangs also serve a practical purpose, providing natural shade in summer and shelter during the colder months.

Green roofs and rainwater retention systems will help manage water across the site, while approximately 1,800 square meters of photovoltaic panels are planned to generate renewable energy. The development is targeting Switzerland’s SNBS Gold sustainability certification.

The winning proposal will now progress through further design and approval stages, with construction of the district’s first buildings possible from 2028. For BIG, which opened its Zurich office in 2023, the project adds another timber-focused development to its growing Swiss portfolio, alongside the planned Dock A terminal at Zurich Airport.

#9115. Ocean liner sunk in Florida to become "world's largest artificial reef"

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach

On Wednesday, the ocean liner SS United States was sunk 180 feet underwater to become an artificial reef off the coast of Florida.

The sinking took approximately eight hours, and dozens of onlookers and officials looked on as the ship underwent a controlled deployment, or scuttling, to the bottom of the ocean.

The ship will join a long stretch of artificial reefs, including 580 other decommissioned vessels and structures, that line the ocean floor off the coast Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida.

“A new chapter has begun in Destin-Fort Walton Beach, Florida, where the legendary SS United States, once the fastest ocean liner in the world, has completed her final voyage to become the World’s Largest Artificial Reef,” said a release from the government of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The site serves as a tourist and dive destination for SCUBA divers both new and seasoned, as the underwater structures are meant to provide infrastructure for marine life.

“Beyond its appeal as a dive destination, the SS United States will serve an important environmental purpose,” said the team.

“Her massive structure will provide new habitat for marine life, supporting the growth of an underwater ecosystem that includes inhabitants such as sea turtles, grouper, snapper and marlin.”

In preparation for its scuttling, the ship underwent a years-long remediation process, where it was stripped of toxic materials, such as green neotex exterior floor covering and paint.

Elements such as the ventilation system, wiring and the propeller were also removed, with the latter stored for a land-based museum that will accompany the dive site.

“To see a project of this magnitude become a reality is an incredible moment for our team and for the future of marine conservation,” said Destin-Fort Walton Beach natural resources chief Alex Fogg.

“This is so much more than creating a new dive destination. It’s an opportunity to advance marine science on a scale we’ve never experienced before. The sheer scale of the SS United States presents a rare opportunity to study how an artificial reef of this size transforms over time.”

The project has been years in the making. The ship, designed by naval architect William Francis Gibb and known for its speed, served as a passenger vessel between 1952 and 1969.

It was decommissioned in 1969, and eventually bought to a Philadelphia harbour in the 1990s, where it sat inactive for decades as various owners bought and then sold the vessel in failed attempts to restore it and make it profitable.

In 2009, the non-profit SS United States Conservancy purchased and began stewarding the ship.

In 2024, due to rent issues, the ship could no longer stay berthed at its Philadelphia pier, and the SS United States Conservancy sold it to Okaloosa County, Florida, for $1 million.

As of today, it stands upright in its intended position, and its uppermost deck is accessible to divers, who can “now enjoy the site”.

Other artificial reefs around the world include the Reefline project in Miami, which is set to feature underwater sculpture designed by OMA and a LEGO-inspired modular system designed by Alex Goad, intended to restore damaged coral reefs.

Photography courtesy of Destin-Fort Walton Beach

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#9111. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#9110. willow defebaugh on the architecture of wonder and what nature teaches us about design

from descartes’ vision of nature as a machine to the principles of biomimicry, the atmos cofounder explores how ecological wisdom can reshape the way we live and design.

The atoms that shiver throughout your being are older than organic life. The elements that bind you together were born in the earliest moments of the universe and forged in faraway stars. The sugars that permit your muscles to move were all made by plants devouring light from a fiery orb. The oxygen that fills your lungs is borrowed from forests and oceans, and the water that makes up most of your body once fell from the sky as drops of rain.

You are constructed of wonder, which is to say nature.

And yet, much of human existence on this planet has been separated from it. The very word we use to describe the sum totality of life is defined by the exclusion of our species. Nature is a learned way of seeing the world as everything that isn’t us. To other anything is the first step to allowing harm, paving the road for extraction and catastrophe. We have bowed out of belonging to the revelry of biological exuberance that is the Earth, and then wonder why we feel lonely.

We can trace the roots of this divide to the Scientific Revolution of 16th- and 17th-century Europe, in which anatomy mapped the body, microscopic life revealed itself, the heavens no longer revolved around us, and gravity was demystified. Alongside these revelations, a new view took shape: nature as a series of mechanical processes, governed by laws that could be observed, understood, and harnessed. And humans, with our uniquely rational minds, were set apart.

Few did more to articulate this perspective than René Descartes. In Discourse on the Method (1637), he described the bodies of animals as machines. He believed that scientific knowledge could allow humans to become “the lords and possessors of nature.” Cartesian dualism was a fissure that cleaved the world in two: mind and matter, thinking subject and physical object. In order to understand the rest of life, we had to observe it from afar.

While Descartes’s cogito ergo sum (“I think, therefore I am”) is widely known, the context is less so. He tied rationalism to doubt: “from the very circumstance that I thought to doubt of the truth of other things, it most clearly and certainly followed that I was.” Doubt, a verb that is so close to wonder, though one houses worry and the other awe. Perhaps rather than doubt leading to thinking to existing, wonder can lead us to feeling to belonging.

Science has taught us extraordinary things about the workings of this world. But to learn how to live within it, we need wisdom.

In the long memory of our planet and the thousands of years in which our species has been living on it, this way of seeing nature as separate from us is a recent phenomenon. The idea that we are separate from nature has never been universal. Many Indigenous cultures have maintained traditions that recognize us as part of the living world, rooted in reciprocity and stewardship. Seeing ourselves as one strand in the web of life is not a new worldview. It’s a very old one.

In Braiding Sweetgrass (2013), botanist and enrolled member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation Robin Wall Kimmerer advocates for a weaving of Indigenous knowledge and Western science. Through stories about plants that plait the personal, cultural, and biological, she illuminates a world in which every growing thing is a guide beckoning us into deeper relationship with the Earth and all of the beings it houses. This is the fertile ground of ecological wisdom.

If knowledge is a collection of facts, wisdom is what we do with it. While science helps us gather knowledge in order to better understand the world we live in, sapience—the possession of wisdom—helps us discern how to move through it. For example, scientific knowledge can reveal that forests exchange nutrients through fungal networks. Ecological wisdom asks what those relationships might teach us about reciprocity, cooperation, and collective well-being.

It’s telling that, while many of us were raised on the importance of science and studied it in school, few of us are taught sapience. Shouldn’t we let everything we have learned about life on Earth guide us in our individual and collective lives? Climate change, biodiversity loss, and ecocide are the evidence of this disconnect, and the wider chasm between us and nature.

This is core to our work at Atmos, a multimedia ecosystem weaving nature into public consciousness. Our mission is to inspire cultural transformation by re-enchanting people with nature. We reveal the ways that human life is interwoven with the Earth, and believe that this connection leads to the solutions that preserve and protect our planet. Our vision is a society in sync with nature’s efficiencies, reciprocities, and beauty. What we offer is proof of wonder.

I have spent the last six years gathering this in the form of a newsletter called The Overview. Rather than liquify in a chrysalis, dragonflies metamorphose incompletely across many moltings. Can we adopt their patience for transformation? Long before humans invented agriculture, ants were farming fungi for food in a way that benefited both. What if our modern agricultural systems could be similarly symbiotic? Hummingbirds can hover, drawing nectar from flowers without ever needing to land on them. Can we learn to live as lightly, leaving so little trace?

In this time, it has become a continuous practice for me to turn to nature for wisdom about how to live. In moving through grief, I turned to ravens and crows, who have been seen holding funerals for the fallen. When struggling with vulnerability, I looked to frogs, who partly breathe through their sensitive skin. Seeking advice on how to navigate the unknown, I found comfort in bats, who make maps of the dark by listening.

In every life form, crawling or winged, scaled or soaring, there are lessons to be found.

At the scale of systems, one of the most direct ways ecological wisdom can guide the way we design our lives is through biomimicry. As Janine Benyus, who popularized the term with her 1997 book, once told me: Every species that is alive today is an example of life having gotten it right—and elegantly so. In our conversation for The Nature Of podcast, she pointed out that our species has a massive design challenge on our hands, but life’s intelligence is all around us.

Bullet trains that take cues from kingfishers, structural color that mirrors the brilliant blue of morpho butterflies rather than synthetic dyes, shark skin-inspired antimicrobial surfaces, temperature regulation modeled after termite mounds—biomimicry provides the blueprints for a designed society that is not separate from, but functionally intertwined with the wonders of the more than human world. It sees every species as a schematic written with possibilities.

Biomimicry is more than taking inspiration from nature or borrowing its aesthetics: it’s about emulating nature’s artistry in both form and function, in a way that gives back to life. As Benyus told me: “Life creates conditions conducive to life.” And we are part of that creative genius. We can design a society that works with nature as we simultaneously remember our place within it.

In World as Lover, World as Self (1991), the late Buddhist and deep ecologist Joanna Macy describes three movements in the story of our species. The first she labeled participation mystique, the state in which one does not distinguish oneself from surrounding objects and the environment. The second was when we left that state and began to see the world as separate, which gave us science but also alienation. The third movement is the one we must now make: back to an awareness of ourselves as part of nature, bringing with us all we have learned.

As Macy put it, “Now it can dawn on us: we are our world knowing itself.”

The root of “eco” is the Greek oikos meaning “home.” We can return to a way of living with this understanding as the foundation already laid, one that reconnects us to the resplendent, abundant aliveness in the garden of life. Our species is standing at the threshold, and ecological wisdom is the key. Outside the house of isolation that we have constructed, home awaits: a circle of belonging as wide as the world. And the architecture of the world is wonder.

Willow Defebaugh is the cofounder and editor-in-chief of Atmos, a climate and culture publication exploring humanity’s relationship with the natural world. Defebaugh is also the author of The Overview, a deep ecology newsletter and book, and the host of The Nature Of podcast.

This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things.
